Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verses 1–6:

﴿By the scatterers, scattering﴾ ﴿and the bearers of burdens, bearing﴾ ﴿and the runners, running with ease﴾ ﴿and the distributors, distributing by command﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ ﴿and indeed, the Judgment is surely to occur﴾

The oath with which it opens is intended to affirm what is sworn to and to emphasize its occurrence. God has sworn by some of His great creations, and in meaning this is an oath by His power and His wisdom. It also includes an honouring of those creations for the blessings and the indications of guidance and goodness in their conditions, and within that is a reminder of God's blessing in what He brought into existence through them.

The things sworn by are attributes, which require their subjects, so the oath returns to being sworn by the subjects for the sake of those great attributes. In this there is a subtle brevity: by omitting the mention of the subjects, there is ample room for what the attributes indicate of suitable subjects, so that the listeners' understanding may go in every possible direction in estimating them.

صفحة ٣٣٧
The coordination of these attributes with (fa, "then") requires their suitability and homogeneity, so they may be attributes of one single class, which is the prevalent case in coordinating attributes with fa, as in the words of Ibn Zayyaba:

"Alas for Zayyaba, for al-Harith the morning-raider, then the one who takes booty, then the one who returns."

It is also possible that their subjects differ, but their subjects are close and homogeneous, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"At the dune-edge of al-Liwa, between al-Dakhul then Hawmal, then Tawdih and then al-Miqra..."

And the words of Labid:

"At the eastern peaks of the two mountains, or at Muhajjar, then Tadammanat-há Fardah, then its rocks... so thunderbolts, if they gleam..." (the verse continues).

This is common in coordinating adjacent places, and it has been mentioned before in the surah al-Saffat.

The early imams differed over the meaning of these attributes and their subjects. The most famous of what is narrated from them is what is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: that the scatterers (al-dhariyat) are the winds, because they scatter the dust; the bearers of burdens (al-hamilat wiqran) are the clouds; the runners (al-jariyat) are the ships; and the distributors by command (al-muqassimat amran) are the angels. This requires that the classes sworn by differ.

Its interpretation is that each thing mentioned first brings to mind what is mentioned after it, through their meeting in an imaginative common ground: the winds recall the clouds, the clouds bearing the weight of water recall the carrying of ships, and all of them recall the angels.

Among the exegetes there are those who made these four attributes a description of the winds. This was said by al-Zamakhshari in the Kashshaf, and part of it is narrated from al-Hasan, and al-Razi approved of it. It is the most suitable for the coordination of the attributes with fa.

صفحة ٣٣٨
The best is to understand scattering (dharw) as the spreading of pieces of cloud in a manner resembling scattering. The real meaning of dharw is throwing gathered things into the air so that they fall to the ground, like seed at sowing or like wool. Its origin is the winds scattering dust, and the pushing of the wind of the pieces of cloud was likened to it, until they gather and become a complete cloud. Thus the scatterers first spread the clouds, as God the Exalted said: ﴿It is God who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky however He wills﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. Although scattering is an attribute of the winds, the fact that what is scattered is a cloud returns to being a state of the clouds. It was also said that their scattering is of dust, and that is before they scatter the clouds, and it is a preliminary to the spreading of the clouds.

The accusative of "dharwan" is the absolute object, to magnify it through tanwin. It may also be a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. "the scattered things," and then its accusative is as the object.

The bearers of burdens (al-hamilat wiqran) are the winds at the time the clouds gather when they have become heavy with water. Their gathering of it is likened to carrying, because it is the nature of a heavy thing to be carried by a carrier. This has the meaning of His words: ﴿and He makes it into fragments, and you see the rain coming out from its midst﴾ [al-Rum: 48], etc., and His words: ﴿and He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12], and His words: ﴿Do you not see that God drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them a heap, and you see the rain coming out from their midst﴾ [al-Nur: 43].

Wiqr, with a kasra on the waw, means a heavy thing.

It is also possible that the bearers are the clouds filled with the vapour of water which becomes rain, coordinated with fa to the scatterers in the sense of the winds, because they arise from them, so they are as if they were them.

The runners with ease (al-jariyat yusran): the winds run with the clouds after their accumulation, when they have become heavy with rainwater. So the sense is: "the one running with that load with ease."

The meaning of yusr is gentleness and ease, i.e. running with a gentle, easy course, like the movement of something laden with weight, as al-A'sha said:

"Her walk from her neighbour's house is like the walk of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty."

So "yusran" is a description of a verbal noun omitted, put in place of the absolute object.

The distributors by command (al-muqassimat amran) are the winds which bring the clouds to the place where what is in the clouds of water reaches its descent, or they are the clouds which send down what is in them of rain upon different places.

Attributing the distribution to them in both senses is metaphorical, by resemblance. It is narrated from al-Hasan that "the distributors" are the clouds through which God divides the provisions of the servants. End of quotation. He means His words: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf: 9] up to His words: ﴿as a provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf: 11] in surah Qaf.

Among the elegance of this interpretation is that there is a correspondence between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to, which is His words: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ ﴿and indeed, the Judgment is surely to occur﴾. The states of the winds mentioned here begin with blowing, then formation, then giving life. Likewise resurrection begins with a blast in the Trumpet, then the reassembling of the bodies of people which had been non-existent or scattered, then the breathing of spirits into them, and behold, they are standing and looking. And His words "by command" may be an indication of what corresponds to it in the example of the causes of life, which is the spirit, according to His words: ﴿Say: the spirit is by the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85].

The "ma" in "innama tu'adun" is a relative pronoun, i.e. "indeed what you are promised is true."

The address in "tu'adun" is to the polytheists, as the emphasis by oath requires, and as His following words require: ﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 8].

So "tu'adun" must be derived from al-wa'id (threat), whose past tense is awʿada, and it is in the passive. The original form of tu'adun was tu'awʿadun, with a fatha-vowelled hamza after the present-tense taʾ and a waw after the hamza, which is the root letter of the verb awʿada, and with a fatha on the ʿayn for the passive form. The hamza was then elided, as is regular in eliding the hamza of "uf'il" in the present tense, like tukrimun, and the waw became dead-vowelled after the damma before it had been live-vowelled, so "tu'adun" arose, its pattern being tufʿalun.

What they were threatened with is the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of this world, such as hunger in the seven lean years, which was the Prophet's ﷺ supplication against them with his words: "O God, make it upon them years like the years of Joseph." This is what His words indicate: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a visible smoke, enveloping people; this is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10–11], in surah al-Dukhan. And such as the punishment of the sword and capture on the day of Badr, which God threatened them with in His words: ﴿On the day We seize with the greatest seizure, indeed We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16].

صفحة ٣٤٠
It is also possible that "tu'adun" is from al-wa'd (promise), i.e. the report of something that will occur in the future, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the promise of God is true﴾ [Yunus: 55], so its pattern is tufʿalun. The intended meaning of al-wa'd is the promise of resurrection.

The description "la-sadiq" (is true) is a metaphor in the rational sense, since what is truly described is the thing promised, as in ﴿So he is in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21].

Al-din means recompense. The intended meaning is the affirmation of the resurrection which they denied.

The sense of "la-waqi'" is: it will occur in the future, by the indication that it is placed in the mention after what they are promised; the occurrence of the promised thing can only be in the future time. Mentioning the recompense, in addition to alluding to it as an affirmation of the resurrection, is an implicit warning of punishment for denying the resurrection.

In the codices, "innama" was written joined, which is contrary to the orthographic convention established afterwards, because the two are two words that did not become one word, unlike "innama" which is for restriction. The orthography at the time the codices were written in the days of Caliph 'Uthman had not yet reached full standardization.

Its origin is the winds scattering dust, and the pushing of the wind of the pieces of cloud was likened to it, until they gather and become a complete cloud. It was also said that their scattering is of dust, and that is before they scatter the clouds, and it is a preliminary to the spreading of the clouds.

Their gathering of it is likened to carrying, because it is the nature of a heavy thing to be carried by a carrier. Wiqr, with a kasra on the waw, means a heavy thing.

It is also possible that the bearers are the clouds filled with the vapour of water which becomes rain, coordinated with fa to the scatterers in the sense of the winds, because they arise from them, so they are as if they were them.

The meaning of yusr is gentleness and ease, i.e. running with a gentle, easy course, like the movement of something laden with weight, as al-A'sha said:

"Her walk from her neighbour's house is like the walk of a cloud, neither slow nor hasty."

So "yusran" is a description of a verbal noun omitted, put in place of the absolute object.

The distributors by command (al-muqassimat amran) are the winds which bring the clouds to the place where what is in the clouds of water reaches its descent, or they are the clouds which send down what is in them of rain upon different places.

Attributing the distribution to them in both senses is metaphorical, by resemblance. It is narrated from al-Hasan that "the distributors" are the clouds through which God divides the provisions of the servants. End of quotation. He means His words: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf: 9] up to His words: ﴿as a provision for the servants﴾ [Qaf: 11] in surah Qaf.

Among the elegance of this interpretation is that there is a correspondence between the thing sworn by and the thing sworn to, which is His words: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ ﴿and indeed, the Judgment is surely to occur﴾. Likewise resurrection begins with a blast in the Trumpet, then the reassembling of the bodies of people which had been non-existent or scattered, then the breathing of spirits into them, and behold, they are standing and looking. And His words "by command" may be an indication of what corresponds to it in the example of the causes of life, which is the spirit, according to His words: ﴿Say: the spirit is by the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85].

Al-din means recompense. The intended meaning is the affirmation of the resurrection which they denied.

This is also an oath, to confirm the disorder of their statements in attacking the religion. It is like a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) of what came before, because what came before was specific to establishing the recompense, whereas this one encompasses the refutation of their misguided statements. So the oath serves to emphasize what is sworn to, since they are unaware of their own state, the state of what the oath is about, and they are eager for more of it. They deny the contradiction and disorder in their statements, while being ignorant of it with a compound ignorance (*jahl murakkab*), and compound ignorance is a denial of sound knowledge.

The discussion of the oath by "the sky" is like the discussion of the oath by *al-Dhariyat*.

The connection of this oath to what is sworn to lies in describing the sky as *dhat al-hubuk*, meaning having paths (*taraʾiq*), because what is sworn to is that their statement is divergent, with paths and sects. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verses 10–11:

﴿Destroyed be the conjecturers,﴾ ﴿those who are heedless in a flood of confusion.﴾

It is a supplication for destruction against the people of that divergent saying, because the intent of "their being killed" is that God destroys them. For this reason it is common to say "qatalahu Allah" (may God fight him), and then it is used in the sense of cursing, belittling, and expressing wonder at the bad state of the one against whom the supplication is made by means of such words.

The sentence of supplication is not conjoined (by a conjunction), because it is very closely connected to what precedes it, of that which necessitated that description, due to their inclusion in this supplication. Just as the succession of the sentence after the sentences before it was an indication that what precedes it is the cause of the supplication against them, and this is from the marvellous (art of) concision.

Al-kharsh (خَرْص): conjecture for which its holder has no proof for his conjecture, so it is exposed to error in his conjecture, and that is a metaphor for going astray, deliberately or through negligence. So "al-kharrasun" (the conjecturers) are the people of the divergent saying, and this indicates that their divergent saying arises from fancies for which there is no evidence. It has already been mentioned in al-An'am: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and they are only guessing﴾ [al-An'am: 116], so what is meant here is conjecture in speech about the Essence of God and His attributes.

Know that khars (conjecture) in the foundations of belief is blameworthy, because they are not built except upon certainty, due to the gravity of their matter, and this is the principal place of blame in this verse.

Page 344
As for khars in dealings between people, it is not blamed in this manner, though some of it is blameworthy when it leads to gambling and speculative risk. Some khars has been permitted out of need. In the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet ﷺ granted a concession regarding the sale of 'ara'ya by its khars" — meaning in the sale of the fruit of the palm-trees given as an 'ariyya. The 'ariyya is the gift by the owner of palm-trees of the fruit of some of his palms to a person for a specified year. The original rule is that he takes its fruit at the time of harvesting the palms. If the owner of the orchard then wishes to buy that fruit before it ripens, it is permitted that the grantee (al-mu'ra, with fatha) sell it to the grantor (al-mu'ri, with kasra) if the grantor wishes that. He estimates (yakhrus) what the palms will bear of fruit, on the basis that he gives him at the harvest what equals that estimated amount, provided it is not large, and it is limited to five awsuq or less, so that the owner of the palms protects his orchard from others' intrusion. This is because its origin is a gift, so no harm enters upon the grantor from it.

Al-ghamrah (الغَمْرَة): the single instance of al-ghamr, which is the mass of water covering things (flood). Its meaning is clarified by what it is annexed to, as in His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming agonies of death﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. When it is not restricted by an annexation, its specification is according to the context, as in His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54] in Surah al-Mu'minun. What is meant is: in preoccupation, that is, what occupies them of enmity toward Islam, an occupation with which they cannot reflect upon the call of the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-sahw (السَّهْو): heedlessness. What is meant is that they are turned away with an aversion like that of the heedless, while they are not heedless, for the call of the Qur'an strikes their ears at every moment. The use of the root sahw in this sense is similar to its use in His saying: ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5].

Know that khars (conjecture) in the foundations of belief is blameworthy, because they are not built except upon certainty, due to the gravity of their matter, and this is the principal place of blame in this verse.

Page 344
As for khars in dealings between people, it is not blamed in this manner, though some of it is blameworthy when it leads to gambling and speculative risk. Some khars has been permitted out of need. In the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet ﷺ granted a concession regarding the sale of 'ara'ya by its khars" — meaning in the sale of the fruit of the palm-trees given as an 'ariyya. The 'ariyya is the gift by the owner of palm-trees of the fruit of some of his palms to a person for a specified year. The original rule is that he takes its fruit at the time of harvesting the palms. If the owner of the orchard then wishes to buy that fruit before it ripens, it is permitted that the grantee (al-mu'ra, with fatha) sell it to the grantor (al-mu'ri, with kasra) if the grantor wishes that. He estimates (yakhrus) what the palms will bear of fruit, on the basis that he gives him at the harvest what equals that estimated amount, provided it is not large, and it is limited to five awsuq or less, so that the owner of the palms protects his orchard from others' intrusion. This is because its origin is a gift, so no harm enters upon the grantor from it.

Al-ghamrah (الغَمْرَة): the single instance of al-ghamr, which is the mass of water covering things (flood). Its meaning is clarified by what it is annexed to, as in His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the overwhelming agonies of death﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. When it is not restricted by an annexation, its specification is according to the context, as in His saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54] in Surah al-Mu'minun. What is meant is: in preoccupation, that is, what occupies them of enmity toward Islam, an occupation with which they cannot reflect upon the call of the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-sahw (السَّهْو): heedlessness. What is meant is that they are turned away with an aversion like that of the heedless, while they are not heedless, for the call of the Qur'an strikes their ears at every moment. The use of the root sahw in this sense is similar to its use in His saying: ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verses 12–14:

﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ ﴿It is the Day when they will be tormented over the Fire.﴾ ﴿"Taste your trial. This is what you were seeking to hasten."﴾

This sentence may be a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "al-Kharraṣūn" (the liars, the conjecturers), or it may be a explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani) arising from the sentence ﴿Killed are the liars﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 10], because the sentence ﴿Killed are the liars﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 10] conveys an expression of wonder at the poor state of their minds and conditions. It therefore provokes a question in the listener's soul that seeks clarification. So it is answered: they ask about the Day of Recompense as mockers, meaning that there is no occurrence of the Day of Recompense, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿About what do they ask one another?﴾ [al-Naba': 1] ﴿About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 2] ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾ [al-Naba': 3].

صفحة ٣٤٥
"Ayyana yawmu al-din" (when is the Day of Recompense) is the object of an omitted verb of saying, indicated by "yas'alūna" (they ask), because the verb of asking contains the meaning of saying. The construction is therefore: they say, "When is the Day of Recompense?" You may also make the sentence "Ayyana yawmu al-din" a substitute (badal) for the clause "yas'alūna," to detail its generality, and this is the type of substitution of agreement (al-badal al-mutabiq).
"Ayyana" is an interrogative noun asking about the time of an event, and it is in a place of accusative (nasb), built on the fatha. That is, "when is the Day of Recompense." The Day of Recompense is a time, so the question about its time returns to a question about its occurrence. The construction is therefore: when is the occurrence of the Day of Recompense, or its arrival, just as you say, "when is the day of Ramadan," meaning when is its beginning, because names of time by right are used as adverbs of events, not of times.

The sentence ﴿The Day when they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ is an answer to their question, following the wise method of meeting a questioner with something other than what he seeks. When they said, "When is the Day of Recompense?", they intended mockery and denial, so their speech is met with something other than their intent, because the answer contains what relieves the impact of their mockery, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: they are times set for people and for the pilgrimage.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189].

The meaning: the Day of Recompense occurs on the Day when you will burn in the Fire, and it will be said to you: "Taste your trial."

﴿The Day when they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and it is the predicate of an omitted subject indicated by the question about it in his saying: "When is the Day of Recompense?"

The construction: the Day of Recompense is the Day when they will be tormented over the Fire.

"Al-fatn" means torment and burning, that is, the Day when they will be tormented by the Fire of Hell. The original sense of "fatn" is testing. Its use has spread to meanings including melting gold over fire in a crucible to test what metal is in it other than gold, which is melted only by intense heat, so here it is a metonymy for intense burning.

The sentence ﴿Taste your trial﴾ is a quoted speech of an omitted verb of saying, indicated by the address, meaning: it will be said to them then, or it is said to them: "Taste your trial," that is, your punishment. The imperative in His saying "taste" is used for rebuke and punishment.

The "dhawq" (tasting) is a metaphor for strong sensation, because the tongue is the most sensitive of the organs.

The idiomatic annexation of "trial" to the pronoun of those addressed on that day is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object. The annexation indicates that it is specific to them, because they deserved it through their disbelief. It is also possible that the annexation is of the verbal noun to its subject. The meaning: taste the recompense of your trial. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, your denial.

From this aspect, it may be understood that the speech is directed to remind the addressees on that day of what they used to inflict on the believers of torment, just as they tried Bilal, Khabbab, 'Ammar, Shumayyah and others. That is, this is the recompense of your trial. The thing tasted is made their trial to show that it is a recompense for their trial of the believers, so that they increase in remorse. God, exalted is He, said, threatening them: ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women and then did not repent will have the punishment of Hell, and they will have the punishment of the burning Fire.﴾ [al-Buruj: 10].

The use of the name of an act for its recompense occurs frequently in the Qur'an, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82], meaning you make the recompense for God's provision to you that you deny His oneness.

The demonstrative in His saying: ﴿This is what you were seeking to hasten﴾ refers to the thing present before their eyes. Such is the usage in similar cases: the masculine form of the demonstrative, as mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is a cow, neither old nor young but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning of ﴿what you were seeking to hasten﴾ [Yunus: 51] is that you used to seek its hastening. The "s" and "t" are for seeking, meaning in the world you used to ask for its hastening, and this is a request by which they meant that this is impossible and will not occur.

Their statements on this are many, which the Qur'an related, like His saying: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48].

The sentence is a resumptive sentence in the context of rebuke and enumeration of crimes, just as it is said to the criminal: "You did such and such," and it is part of the speech that is said.

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿taking what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were, before that, doers of good,﴾ ﴿sleeping little of the night,﴾ ﴿and in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness,﴾ ﴿and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived.﴾

This is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical sentence inserted into the discourse), in which the state of the believers on the Day of Judgment is set against the state of the disbelievers. It follows the Qur'an's usual method of pairing warning with good tidings, and intimidation with encouragement.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾, is similar to his saying in Surat al-Dukhan: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure place, in gardens and springs﴾.

He used the plural "gardens" (*jannāt*) in agreement with the plural "the God-fearing," and they are many different gardens. In a hadith: "Indeed, they are many gardens, and he is in al-Firdaws." The indefiniteness of "gardens" (*jannāt*) signifies magnificence.

The meaning of ﴿taking what their Lord has given them﴾ is that they accept what He has given them, that is, they are content with it. The verb "taking" (*akhdh*) is used both in its literal sense and in a figurative sense, a *kināya* (indirect expression) in the sense of a symbolic allusion to the fact that what they are given is the most perfect of its kind. This is because the perceptions of groups differ in their appreciation of things, until something reaches the utmost degree of excellence, whereupon people agree on its excellence. This is a *kināya talwīḥiyya* (an allusive indirect expression).

Also, the verb "taking" is used in its literal and metaphorical senses, because some of what God gives them can be grasped by the hand, such as fruits, drinks and fragrant plants, while other things cannot be grasped by the hand, such as beautiful sights, delicate sounds, honor and divine good pleasure. The latter is more numerous than the former.

Thus the application of the verb "taking" to these things is a *istiʿāra* (metaphor) that likens the intelligible to the perceptible, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ in Surat al-Baqara, and His saying: ﴿Command your people to take the best of it﴾ in Surat al-A'raf.

Thus two indirect expressions and a metaphor are combined in the word "taking" (*ākhidhīn*). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that God, Exalted is He, says: "O people of Paradise!" They say: "At your service, our Lord, and at your pleasure, and all good is in Your hands." He says: "Are you content?" They say: "And why would we not be content, our Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?" He says: "Shall I not give you something better than that?"

[Page 348]

They say: "And what could be better than that?" He says: "I will cause My good pleasure to descend upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you after this, ever."

In the choice of expressing the Majesty by the attribute "Lord" (*rabb*), in the form of an annexed noun with the pronoun of "the God-fearing," there is a meaning of their being singled out for honor, and an allusion that the cause of what He has given them is their faith in His lordship, which belongs specifically to them, and this corresponds to the attributes of God, Exalted is He, in reality.

The clause ﴿Indeed, they were, before that, doers of good﴾ is a justification for the clause ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾. That is, this was a recompense for them for their good deeds, just as it was said to the polytheists: "Taste your trial." The *muḥsinūn* (doers of good) are those who perform good deeds, which are acts of obedience.

The benefit of the adverbial phrase in His saying "before that" is that the reference is made to what has been mentioned of gardens, springs and what their Lord has given them, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard and no human heart has conceived. Through this reference, the magnitude of the thing referred to is magnified. Then, by His saying "before that," it is conveyed, that is, before enjoying it, that they were doers of good, that is, performers of good deeds, as His saying explains it: ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾, etc. The meaning is that in this world they were obedient to God, Exalted is He, trusting in His promise, though they had not seen Him.

The clause ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾ is a *badal* (substitution) for the clause ﴿they were, before that, doers of good﴾, a *badal baʿḍ min kull* (substitution of a part for a whole), because these three qualities are a part of good conduct in action. This is like an example of their greatest goodness, for what is mentioned of their deeds indicates the intensity of their obedience to God, seeking His good pleasure, by exerting the utmost effort that can be exerted upon the self, and that is two things.

The first is rest for the self at a time when its need for rest is most pressing, and this is the whole night, especially its last part, when the one who stands in prayer at night has become exhausted and his need for rest has become acute.

The second is wealth, which souls usually cling to tightly. These four deeds include the two foundations of reforming the self and reforming people. This is the sum of what the obligations of religious duty aim at, for the reform of the self is the purification of the inner and outer being. In standing in prayer at night there is an indication of the purification of the self through seeking the pleasure of God, Exalted is He. In seeking forgiveness there is the purification of the outer being through good words that bring about the good pleasure of God, Mighty and Majestic.

[Page 349]

In their placing of the right in their wealth for the beggars, there is clear benefit for the needy one who makes his need known. In their placing of the right for the deprived, there is benefit for the needy one who keeps himself from showing his need, who endures the severity of his need.

The particle *mā* in His saying ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾ is an emphatic addition. It has become common to add *mā* after the nouns "little" (*qalīl*) and "much" (*kathīr*), and after the verbs "was few" (*qalla*), "was many" (*kathura*) and "was long" (*ṭāla*).

The meaning is: they used to sleep a little of the night. And *mā* here is not a negation.

The *hujūʿ* (sleep) is light sleep, and it is the *ghirār* (light dozing).

The verse indicates that they used to sleep a little of the night, and this is following the command of God, Exalted is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ) in His saying: "Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it." The Prophet (ﷺ) used to command them to do so, as in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that the Messenger of God said to him: "I was told that you stand in prayer at night and fast during the day." He said: "Yes." He said: "Do not do so. Indeed, if you do so, your soul will become weary and your eyes will become sunken. Rather, stand in prayer and sleep, for your self has a right over you and your family has a right over you."

This sentence contains several features of eloquence.

The first is the verb of being, "they were" (*kānū*), which indicates that its predicate is an established practice.

The second is the deviation from saying "they used to stand the night in prayer," or "they used to pray in the middle of the night," to His saying "sleeping little of the night," because mentioning sleep serves as a reminder of the state to which souls incline, and which overpowers them and turns them away from the remembrance of God, Exalted is He. This is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾. So there is in the verse a *iṭnāb* (elaboration) required by the depiction of that state, and the eloquent speaker may include in his speech what the understanding of the meaning does not depend upon, when he intends by that to achieve the forms of the additional expressions.

The third is the explicit statement of "of the night" (*min al-layl*), as a reminder that they gave up sleep at the time when it is naturally in the souls' inclination to sleep, as an added enhancement in depicting the magnificence of their standing in prayer at night. Otherwise, His saying "they were sleeping little" would already indicate that it is of the night.

[Page 350]

The verb "taking" (*akhdh*) is used both in its literal sense and in a figurative sense, a *kināya* (indirect expression) in the sense of a symbolic allusion to the fact that what they are given is the most perfect of its kind. This is because the perceptions of groups differ in their appreciation of things, until something reaches the utmost degree of excellence, whereupon people agree on its excellence. This is a *kināya talwīḥiyya* (an allusive indirect expression).

Also, the verb "taking" is used in its literal and metaphorical senses, because some of what God gives them can be grasped by the hand, such as fruits, drinks and fragrant plants, while other things cannot be grasped by the hand, such as beautiful sights, delicate sounds, honor and divine good pleasure. The latter is more numerous than the former.

Thus the application of the verb "taking" to these things is a *istiʿāra* (metaphor) that likens the intelligible to the perceptible, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ in Surat al-Baqara, and His saying: ﴿Command your people to take the best of it﴾ in Surat al-A'raf.

Thus two indirect expressions and a metaphor are combined in the word "taking" (*ākhidhīn*). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that God, Exalted is He, says: "O people of Paradise!" They say: "At your service, our Lord, and at your pleasure, and all good is in Your hands." He says: "Are you content?" They say: "And why would we not be content, our Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?" He says: "Shall I not give you something better than that?"

[Page 348]

They say: "And what could be better than that?" He says: "I will cause My good pleasure to descend upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you after this, ever."

The clause ﴿Indeed, they were, before that, doers of good﴾ is a justification for the clause ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾. That is, this was a recompense for them for their good deeds, just as it was said to the polytheists: "Taste your trial." The *muḥsinūn* (doers of good) are those who perform good deeds, which are acts of obedience.

Through this reference, the magnitude of the thing referred to is magnified. Then, by His saying "before that," it is conveyed, that is, before enjoying it, that they were doers of good, that is, performers of good deeds, as His saying explains it: ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾, etc. The meaning is that in this world they were obedient to God, Exalted is He, trusting in His promise, though they had not seen Him.

This is like an example of their greatest goodness, for what is mentioned of their deeds indicates the intensity of their obedience to God, seeking His good pleasure, by exerting the utmost effort that can be exerted upon the self, and that is two things.

The first is rest for the self at a time when its need for rest is most pressing, and this is the whole night, especially its last part, when the one who stands in prayer at night has become exhausted and his need for rest has become acute.

The second is wealth, which souls usually cling to tightly. These four deeds include the two foundations of reforming the self and reforming people. This is the sum of what the obligations of religious duty aim at, for the reform of the self is the purification of the inner and outer being. In standing in prayer at night there is an indication of the purification of the self through seeking the pleasure of God, Exalted is He. In seeking forgiveness there is the purification of the outer being through good words that bring about the good pleasure of God, Mighty and Majestic.

[Page 349]

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿taking what their Lord has given them. This is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical sentence inserted into the discourse), in which the state of the believers on the Day of Judgment is set against the state of the disbelievers. It follows the Qur'an's usual method of pairing warning with good tidings, and intimidation with encouragement.

He used the plural "gardens" (*jannāt*) in agreement with the plural "the God-fearing," and they are many different gardens. In a hadith: "Indeed, they are many gardens, and he is in al-Firdaws." The indefiniteness of "gardens" (*jannāt*) signifies magnificence.

The meaning of ﴿taking what their Lord has given them﴾ is that they accept what He has given them, that is, they are content with it. The verb "taking" (*akhdh*) is used both in its literal sense and in a figurative sense, a *kināya* (indirect expression) in the sense of a symbolic allusion to the fact that what they are given is the most perfect of its kind. This is because the perceptions of groups differ in their appreciation of things, until something reaches the utmost degree of excellence, whereupon people agree on its excellence. This is a *kināya talwīḥiyya* (an allusive indirect expression).

Also, the verb "taking" is used in its literal and metaphorical senses, because some of what God gives them can be grasped by the hand, such as fruits, drinks and fragrant plants, while other things cannot be grasped by the hand, such as beautiful sights, delicate sounds, honor and divine good pleasure. The latter is more numerous than the former.

Thus the application of the verb "taking" to these things is a *istiʿāra* (metaphor) that likens the intelligible to the perceptible, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ in Surat al-Baqara, and His saying: ﴿Command your people to take the best of it﴾ in Surat al-A'raf.

Thus two indirect expressions and a metaphor are combined in the word "taking" (*ākhidhīn*). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that God, Exalted is He, says: "O people of Paradise!" They say: "At your service, our Lord, and at your pleasure, and all good is in Your hands." He says: "Are you content?" They say: "And why would we not be content, our Lord, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?" He says: "Shall I not give you something better than that?"

[Page 348]

They say: "And what could be better than that?" He says: "I will cause My good pleasure to descend upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you after this, ever."

In the choice of expressing the Majesty by the attribute "Lord" (*rabb*), in the form of an annexed noun with the pronoun of "the God-fearing," there is a meaning of their being singled out for honor, and an allusion that the cause of what He has given them is their faith in His lordship, which belongs specifically to them, and this corresponds to the attributes of God, Exalted is He, in reality.

The clause ﴿Indeed, they were, before that, doers of good﴾ is a justification for the clause ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾. That is, this was a recompense for them for their good deeds, just as it was said to the polytheists: "Taste your trial." The *muḥsinūn* (doers of good) are those who perform good deeds, which are acts of obedience.

The benefit of the adverbial phrase in His saying "before that" is that the reference is made to what has been mentioned of gardens, springs and what their Lord has given them, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard and no human heart has conceived. Through this reference, the magnitude of the thing referred to is magnified. Then, by His saying "before that," it is conveyed, that is, before enjoying it, that they were doers of good, that is, performers of good deeds, as His saying explains it: ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾, etc. The meaning is that in this world they were obedient to God, Exalted is He, trusting in His promise, though they had not seen Him.

The clause ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾ is a *badal* (substitution) for the clause ﴿they were, before that, doers of good﴾, a *badal baʿḍ min kull* (substitution of a part for a whole), because these three qualities are a part of good conduct in action. This is like an example of their greatest goodness, for what is mentioned of their deeds indicates the intensity of their obedience to God, seeking His good pleasure, by exerting the utmost effort that can be exerted upon the self, and that is two things.

The first is rest for the self at a time when its need for rest is most pressing, and this is the whole night, especially its last part, when the one who stands in prayer at night has become exhausted and his need for rest has become acute.

The second is wealth, which souls usually cling to tightly. These four deeds include the two foundations of reforming the self and reforming people. This is the sum of what the obligations of religious duty aim at, for the reform of the self is the purification of the inner and outer being. In standing in prayer at night there is an indication of the purification of the self through seeking the pleasure of God, Exalted is He. In seeking forgiveness there is the purification of the outer being through good words that bring about the good pleasure of God, Mighty and Majestic.

[Page 349]

In their placing of the right in their wealth for the beggars, there is clear benefit for the needy one who makes his need known. In their placing of the right for the deprived, there is benefit for the needy one who keeps himself from showing his need, who endures the severity of his need.

The particle *mā* in His saying ﴿sleeping little of the night﴾ is an emphatic addition. It has become common to add *mā* after the nouns "little" (*qalīl*) and "much" (*kathīr*), and after the verbs "was few" (*qalla*), "was many" (*kathura*) and "was long" (*ṭāla*).

The meaning is: they used to sleep a little of the night. And *mā* here is not a negation.

The *hujūʿ* (sleep) is light sleep, and it is the *ghirār* (light dozing).

The verse indicates that they used to sleep a little of the night, and this is following the command of God, Exalted is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ) in His saying: "Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce it a little, or add to it." The Prophet (ﷺ) used to command them to do so, as in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that the Messenger of God said to him: "I was told that you stand in prayer at night and fast during the day." He said: "Yes." He said: "Do not do so. Indeed, if you do so, your soul will become weary and your eyes will become sunken. Rather, stand in prayer and sleep, for your self has a right over you and your family has a right over you."

This sentence contains several features of eloquence.

The first is the verb of being, "they were" (*kānū*), which indicates that its predicate is an established practice.

The second is the deviation from saying "they used to stand the night in prayer," or "they used to pray in the middle of the night," to His saying "sleeping little of the night," because mentioning sleep serves as a reminder of the state to which souls incline, and which overpowers them and turns them away from the remembrance of God, Exalted is He. This is of the same kind as His saying: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾. So there is in the verse a *iṭnāb* (elaboration) required by the depiction of that state, and the eloquent speaker may include in his speech what the understanding of the meaning does not depend upon, when he intends by that to achieve the forms of the additional expressions.

The third is the explicit statement of "of the night" (*min al-layl*), as a reminder that they gave up sleep at the time when it is naturally in the souls' inclination to sleep, as an added enhancement in depicting the magnificence of their standing in prayer at night. Otherwise, His saying "they were sleeping little" would already indicate that it is of the night.

[Page 350]

The fourth is the restriction of sleep to "little," to indicate that they do not complete the full limit of the reality of sleep, but take only a little of it. This particularity escaped Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat in his saying:

The helmet has shaved my head bare, so I taste no sleep except light dozing.

The fifth is the exaggeration in minimizing their sleep, to convey that it is the least a sleeper can sleep.

The word "little" (*qalīlan*) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, because it is qualified as a time by His saying "of the night." The implied sense is: a little time of the night, and the governing element of the adverb is "they sleep." And "of the night" here is partitive.

Then He followed this with the statement that they seek forgiveness at dawn (*al-saḥar*), that is, when the night begins to end, they ask God to forgive them after they have offered in advance from the night prayer what they hope will bring them near to the good pleasure of God, Exalted is He.

This indicates that their sleep, which occurs during the course of the night, is before the dawn. As for the time of dawn, they are then performing the night prayer (*tahajjud*). For this reason, Ibn Umar and Mujahid interpreted the seeking of forgiveness as prayer at dawn. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾. The intended meaning is not merely seeking forgiveness with the tongue, even if the one seeking forgiveness is in his bed, for in that case no special merit would appear in restricting the seeking of forgiveness to the time of dawn.

The *asḥār* (dawns) is the plural of *saḥar*, which is the end of the night. This time was singled out because at it sleep commonly overcomes a person, so their prayer and their seeking of forgiveness at that time is more remarkable than their prayer in other portions of the night.

The plural *asḥār* is used in view of the repetition of their standing in prayer at every dawn.

The placement of "at dawn" (*bil-asḥār*) before "they seek forgiveness" is for the sake of emphasis on it, as you have understood.

Their seeking of forgiveness is expressed in the style of stating the subject explicitly rather than by a pronoun, in order to show the high regard in which they are held, and so that the report about the subject is made by a verbal predicate, which conveys the strengthening of the report. For the seeking of forgiveness at dawn is so rare that it calls for emphasis, since seeking forgiveness at dawn is burdensome for the one who stands in prayer at night, because that is the time of his exhaustion.

This construction follows the pattern of the saying: "He gives abundantly."

The right of the beggar and the deprived is the portion they give to them. It is on this basis that the statement of one who said that this right is zakat is to be interpreted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 20:

[Page 352]
﴿And on the earth are signs for those who have certainty.﴾
This is connected to the oath and its answer, from His saying ﴿By those that scatter [dust]﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 1] and His saying ﴿By the sky having paths﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 7], up to His saying ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 5] and ﴿And indeed, the judgment is to occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 6]. So, after He established the occurrence of the Resurrection by emphasizing it with the oath, He moved on to bringing it closer through evidence, in order to refute their deeming it impossible. This argument is like His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revived it is the Reviver of the dead﴾ [Fussilat: 39].

Between these two sentences lies a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). The sentence ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who have certainty﴾ may be coordinated (ma'tufah) with the sentence that is the answer to the oath, namely ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 5]. The meaning is: and in what is observed of the conditions of the earth are signs for those who have certainty, namely the conditions that indicate the bringing into existence of beings after the annihilation of their likes and origins, such as the sprouting of new crops after the previous ones have perished and become dry stubble.

These are clear, recurring proofs that do not require the exertion of deep thought; for this reason these signs were not joined with anything that calls for reflection, as His saying ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21] was joined.

Know that the signs visible in the conditions of the earth are also suitable to indicate His exaltedness being the sole deity, in the manner of its creation and spreading out for living beings and humankind, and how it was divided into plains, mountains and seas, and the order of its causing grains and trees to grow, and what benefits for people come forth from that. For this reason the signs were left without a restricting complement, so that they encompass everything the signs in the earth are fit to indicate.

The fronting of the predicate in His saying "And on the earth" is for emphasis and to arouse anticipation for the mention of the subject.

The lam in "for those who have certainty" is attached to "signs." The signs were specified for "those who have certainty" because they are the ones who benefited from their indication, so the signs bestowed upon them certainty about the occurrence of the Resurrection. The description "those who have certainty" is preferred here over "those who are certain" to convey that they were known for certainty. This description implies praise of them for keen understanding, since certainty comes only from evidence, and the proofs of this matter are speculative (nazariyyah). It also praises them for fairness and for abandoning obstinacy, since most of those who deny the truth are driven by obstinacy or envy, rejecting the truth of one whom they fear will undermine their interests.

[Page 353]
The fronting of "in the earth" before the subject is for the sake of attention to the earth, considering it as many signs.

The phrase is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical conjunction) with "in the earth" (*fī al-arḍ*). The full sense is: "And in yourselves are signs; will you not see?" The verse-ending is therefore to be paused on "in yourselves" (*anfusikum*). The prepositional phrase cannot be taken as dependent on "you see" (*tubṣirūn*) and placed before it, because the presence of the particle *fa* (then/so) prevents this, since the sentence would then be conjoined by two particles. The address is directed at the polytheists (*mushrikūn*).

The interrogative is a denial (*istifhām inkārī*, a rhetorical question expressing rejection): it denounces them for not seeing the signs.

"Seeing" (*al-ibṣār*) is used metaphorically (*mustaʿār*) for reflection and contemplation (*tadabbur wa-tafakkur*), meaning: how can you abandon considering signs that exist within yourselves?

Placing "in yourselves" before its complement serves to draw attention to considering the creation of their own selves, and also to accommodate the verse-ending (*fāṣilah*, the rhymed final unit of the verse).

The meaning is: Do you not reflect upon the creation of your selves: how God brought you into being from water, and how He created you in stages (*aṭwāran*)? Is it not the case that every stage is the bringing into existence of a creation that did not exist before? What exists in the child did not exist in him when he was a fetus; what exists in the grown man did not exist in him when he was a youth. Upon reflection, these are nothing but newly produced creatures that were non-existent, and so likewise is the completion of creation after death.

This wondrous formation, just as it indicates the possibility of bringing into existence after death, also indicates that its Maker, exalted is He, is unique in divinity, for none other than God Almighty is able to create the like of a human being. The inner and outer states of a human being are wonders of order and harmony, and the most marvellous of them are: the creation of the intellect and its operations and the extraction of meanings; the creation of speech and the innate inspiration toward language; the creation of the senses; the movement of the blood circulation; the coordination of the principal organs and their interaction; the arrangement of the joints, the muscles, the nerves and the arteries, and their state between slackness and dryness. For when dryness predominates over them, incapacity comes, and when slackness predominates, death comes.

[Page 354]

The address is to those who were addressed at the beginning of the surah with the words of God: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ (51:5).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 22:

﴿And in the heaven is your provision, and that which you are promised.﴾

After mentioning the signs in the earth and the signs in the souls, which are among the things connected to the earth, he turned to mention the heaven for the sake of relevance, and as a preparation for the oath that follows it in His saying ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 23]. And because in the heaven there is the sign of the rain, by which the earth brings forth plants after its dryness, the meaning is: in the heaven is the sign of the rain. He turned away from mentioning the rain to mentioning the provision (rizq), incorporating the favour (imtinan) into the argument, since the proof lies in its being rain that gives life to the earth after its death. This is an analogical comparison (qiyas tamthil) for vegetation, i.e., in the heaven is the rain by means of which you are provided for.

So the provision (rizq) is the rain carried by the clouds, and the heaven here means the layers of the atmosphere.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) before what it modifies (muta'allaq) is for creating suspense, for giving importance to the place, and for responding to the fasila (verse-end rhyme).

The conjunction of ﴿wa ma tu'adun﴾ is an incorporation (idmaj) among the proofs of the establishment of the Resurrection, for the purpose of an admonition that comprehends both the warning (wa'id) regarding polytheism and the promise (wa'd) regarding faith, if they believe, hastening the admonition at the moment its opportunity arises.

In the choice of the form ﴿tu'adun﴾ there is a particularity among the features of the miraculous nature (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, for this form is suitable to be derived from the root wa'd (promise), in which case the pattern of ﴿tu'adun﴾ is tuf'alun, the imperfect of wa'ada in the passive voice. Its original form before being put into the passive was ta'idun, and its origin was tu'idun; then when it was put into the passive, the prefixed letter of the imperfect was dammed, so the quiescent waw became a madda harmonizing with the damma, and it became tu'adun.

And it is suitable to be derived from the root i'ad (threat), whose pattern is ta'af'alun, following the conjugation of akrama yukrimu; and with this, tu'adun became like tukramun, so it admits both good tidings (bishara) and warning (infar).

That this is in the heaven may mean that it is established in the knowledge of the people of the heaven, i.e., the angels entrusted with directing it.
It may also mean that the place of its occurrence is in the heaven, from a Garden or Hell, based on the view that the Garden and Hell already exist before the Day of Resurrection; there is disagreement on this which does not need to be mentioned.

In it is also an allusion that what they were threatened with will come to them from the direction of the heaven, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So watch for the day when the heaven brings forth a visible smoke, covering the people; this is a painful punishment﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 10]. That smoke was in the layers of the atmosphere, as was mentioned earlier in the surah ad-Dukhan.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 51, verse 23:**

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is surely true, just as it is true that you speak.﴾ After he had emphasized the speech with an oath by *al-Dhāriyāt* (the scattering winds) and what is conjoined with it, he followed this with a further emphasis by an oath by the Creator of the heaven and the earth, that what you are promised is true. It is thus a continuation of the preceding speech, and its connection is his saying, "And what you are promised."

The explicit mention of "the heaven and the earth," rather than referring to them by pronoun, serves to instill awe in the hearts of the listeners through the greatness of the Lord, glorified is He.

The pronoun in "indeed it is surely true" refers back to "what you are promised." This is an instance of *radd al-ʿajz ʿalā al-ṣadr* (a rhetorical device in which the end of a passage echoes its beginning), for it responds to His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely true﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 5]. And the purpose has been completed.

His saying ﴿just as it is true that you speak﴾ is an added confirmation of the occurrence of what they were promised, by likening it to something known, like a necessity, about which there is no doubt in its occurrence, namely that the addressees speak. This is similar to their saying: "Just as before today is yesterday," or "Just as after today is tomorrow." It is among the examples drawn from sensible matters, and among it is the illustration of the swiftness of arrival by the nearness of the place, in the verse of Zuhayr:

*So they and the valley of al-Rass are like the hand to the mouth.*

And their saying: "Just as you are here," and their saying: "Just as you see and hear."

Page 356

The majority of readers recited *mithla* (مِثْلَ) in the accusative, considering it an adverbial qualifier of an omitted *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), intended for emphasis. The sense is: "Indeed, it is surely true, a truth just as it is true that you speak."

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr (from ʿĀṣim), and Khalaf recited *laḥaqqun* (لَحَقٌّ) in the nominative, as an adjective, with the intention of likening.

The *mā* (ما) that follows *mithla* (مِثْلَ) is superfluous (*zāʾida*), for emphasis. It is followed by *anna* (أنَّ), which conveys emphasis, to strengthen the affirmation of the truth of what they are promised.

The present tense in *tanṭiqūna* (تَنْطِقُونَ), rather than saying *nuṭquKum* (نُطْقُكم), conveys the comparison with their speech as continually renewed, and this is stronger in occurrence because it is perceptible.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verses 24–30:

﴿Has there come to you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, [you are] a people unknown [to me]."﴾ ﴿Then he turned quickly to his household and brought a fattened calf.﴾ ﴿And he set it before them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿So he felt within himself apprehension of them. They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a learned boy.﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry and struck her face and said, "[I am] an old barren woman!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus has your Lord said. Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing."﴾

This is a transition from warning, admonition and argument to taking lesson from the states of earlier nations that resemble the polytheists addressed in their disbelief and their denial of the messengers. The sentence is a fresh, independent beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the style of speech shifts from direct address to the warners to an indirect style (ta'ridh), as a variation (tafannun) by mentioning the story of Abraham, to serve as a preface (tawti'ah) to the intended matter, which is the mention of what befell the people of Lot when they denied their messenger. Thus the intended point is what follows His saying: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 31].

Beginning with the mention of the people of Lot in this verse was contrary to the order that the Qur'an's usage followed in arranging the stories of the denying nations, which begin with the people of Noah, then 'Ad, then Thamud, then the people of Lot. The reason for the transition from the threat against the polytheists to the lesson of the earlier nations is that the polytheists were described just before as being "in heedlessness, neglectful" (ghamrah sahun), so in that heedlessness they were more akin to the people of Lot, of whom God said: ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾ [al-Hijr: 72]. Also, the punishment with which the people of Lot were punished was stones sent down upon them from the sky, likened to rain. It was named "rain" in His saying: ﴿And they had certainly passed by the town which was rained upon with a rain of evil﴾ [al-Furqan: 40], and His saying: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. Moreover, in the story of the angels' presence with Abraham and his wife there is a lesson on the possibility of resurrection, for it includes the good tidings of a child who would be born to her after despair of childbearing; and that is like resurrection to life after death.

When the address was directed to the Prophet ﷺ with His saying "Has there come to you," it is understood that the primary purpose is to console him for what he met from his people's denial. Following from this is an indirect allusion to the hearers when the Qur'an is recited to them or he conveys to them that they are destined for a similar punishment, because the causes are the same.

The expression "Has there come to you" has already been discussed in the parallel at His saying: ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ [Sad: 21] in Surah Sad, and that such an expression introduces grand and important reports.

Al-dayf (the guest): a noun used for the singular and the plural, since its origin is the verbal noun of dhaafa, meaning "to incline," and it was applied to one who inclines toward someone's house to stay with him. Then it became a noun; when its origin is considered, it is applied to the singular and to others, and they do not make it feminine or plural; and when the noun itself is considered, they make it plural for groups and feminine for females, so they say adyaf and duyuf, and dayfah for a female guest. Here it is a collective noun (ism jam'), and therefore it is described by "the honored ones." It was discussed in Surah al-Hijr: ﴿He said, "Indeed, these are my guests"﴾ [al-Hijr: 68].

What is meant by them are the angels whom God made manifest to Abraham, peace be upon him, and who informed him that they were sent from God to carry out the punishment upon the people of Lot. God called them "guests" in view of the form of their coming in the appearance of guests, just as He called the two angels who came to Dawud "adversaries" in His saying: ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ [Sad: 21]; this is a formal metaphor (isti'arah suwariyyah).

In the Book of Genesis of the Torah, they were three. From Ibn 'Abbas: they were Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil. From 'Ata': Jibril, Mika'il, and with them another angel.

Perhaps the reason for sending three was that they would take the form of men, as people customarily know in their journeys that a caravan of travellers is not fewer than three companions. That is the origin of the address being in the dual form, as in: (qifa nabki). And in a hadith: "One is a devil, two are two devils, and three are a caravan." Narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, who said its chain is sahih.

It may also be that the reason for their being sent as three is that the punishment of the people of Lot was of different kinds, and each kind had its own angel assigned to it.

Describing them as "honored" is an oblique statement, for it gives the impression that this was for Abraham's honoring them, as was his custom with guests, and he was the one who established hospitality. The intended meaning is that God honored them by elevating their rank, for the angels are near to God, as He said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26], and He said: ﴿Noble writers﴾ [al-Infitar: 11].

The adverbial clause "when they entered upon him" is connected to "news" because it contains the sense of a verb, meaning: their report when they entered upon him.

His saying ﴿They said, "Peace," he said, "Peace"﴾ has a parallel discussed in Surah Hud. The majority read "qala salamun" (he said, "Peace"). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "qala silmun," with a kasrah on the sin and sukun on the lam.

His saying ﴿"[You are] a people unknown"﴾ is part of Abraham's speech. The apparent view is that he said it quietly, since it is not part of honoring a visitor to voice that openly to him. So the implied sense is: "They are a people unknown."

Al-munkar: one whose state is disliked by another, meaning not known. Here it is applied to one whose condition is unfamiliar and is thought to be an unusual state, that is, one feared to harbor evil, as He said in Surah Hud: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he found them strange and felt apprehension of them﴾ [Hud: 70]. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She disliked me, and what she disliked of the events was nothing but my grey hair and my baldness,"
meaning: she disliked my person.

The story of Abraham's guests has been discussed in Surah Hud.

"Raagha" means to incline sideways while walking, from which comes "rawaghan al-tha'lab" (the fox's dodging). The meaning is that Abraham turned aside from the place where the guests had alighted to his household, that is, to his house in which his family was.

In the Torah, he was sitting before the door of his tent under a tree, and he had brought the guests down beneath the tree.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam said: "raghan" is a deviation in walking from straightness toward a side while concealing that intention. Al-Raghib, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him in this restriction. From it al-Zamakhshari drew that Abraham's concealment of his inclination toward his household was part of good hospitality, so that he would not give the guest the impression that he intended to bring them something, lest the guest hold him back from that and excuse him. This is a subtle point.

The lodging of Abraham where this story took place was in a place called (Bulutat Mamra) in the land of Jabrun.

The calf is described here as "fattened" (samin), while in Surah Hud it is described as "roasted" (hanidh), that is, grilled; so it was a fattened calf which he grilled and set before them. Grilling was the quickest cooking of the desert people. Imru' al-Qays said, describing the hunt:

"So the cooks of meat stayed, between one who ripened the roast in slices and one who hastened the pot."

He restricted "pot" (qadir) with "hastened" (mu'ajjal), but did not restrict "slices of roast" (saffiyat shiwa'), because it is known.

The meaning of "qarrabahu" (he set it near them) is that he placed it close to them, that is, he did not move them from their seat to another place, but placed the food before them. This is part of completing honor for the guest, unlike what the one who seeks food or the beggar is given, for he is called to the place of the food, as al-Farazdaq said:

"I said, 'To the food,' and among them a group who envy the companionable one, the food."

The coming of the particle fa' to conjoin the verbs "fara'a," "fa-ja'a," "fa-qarrabahu" indicates that these actions happened swiftly, and hastening with hospitality is part of complete generosity, and it has been said: "The best of charity is that which is quickest."

The clause ﴿He said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ is a substitute clause (badal ishtimal) for the clause "he set it near them."

"Ala" is one word, and it is a particle of invitation (harf 'ard), that is, a desire for the act to take place that it precedes. Here it is definitely an invitation, because the verb of saying falls as a substitute for the verb "qarrabahu ilayhim," and it is not good to make it two words of interrogative hamzah for denial with the negative "la."

Offering food to the guest right after placing it before him is an increase in honor, by showing eagerness for what benefits the guest, even though placing the food before him is sufficient for enabling him to eat it. This has been considered by the jurists as permission for accepting invitations to banquets, as opposed to merely the existence of a table of food or a provision-cloth, since it may have been prepared for someone other than the invited guest.

The fa' in ﴿So he felt within himself apprehension of them﴾ is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasihah), because it discloses an implied sentence required by the connection of meaning, that is: "They did not eat, so he felt within himself apprehension of them," like His saying: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 63]. This was made explicit in Surah Hud: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾ [Hud: 70], that is, toward the calf, ﴿he found them strange and felt apprehension of them﴾ [Hud: 70].

"Awjasa" means he sensed in his self and did not show it; its parallel was discussed in Surah Hud.

Their saying to him "Fear not" is because they knew what was in his self from the fear that appeared on his features; its parallel was discussed in Surah Hud.

The boy they gave him good tidings of is Isaac, because he is the son of Sarah, and it is he whose good tidings occur in this story in the Torah. He is described here as "learned" ('alim). As for the one whose good tidings are mentioned in Surah al-Saffat, he is Ishmael, described as "forbearing" (halim). Therefore the wife of Abraham spoken of here is Sarah, who gave birth after she had despaired; as for Hagar, she was a young girl who bore a child in the beginning of her life. The wife came forward when she heard the good tidings of a boy for her, that is, she came toward the gathering of Abraham with his guests. God said in Surah Hud: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾ [Hud: 71].

Women used to attend men's gatherings in their homes with their husbands and eat with them. In the Muwatta', Malik said: "There is no harm in a woman attending with her husband and his guest and eating with them."

"Sarrah" is a cry, and from it the word "sarir" (a shrill sound) is derived.

The "fi" here is for the figurative sense of containment, which is accompaniment.

"Sakk" is slapping, and striking the face in astonishment was the custom of women in that time. Its parallel is placing the hand over the mouth in His saying: ﴿So they put their hands over their mouths﴾ [Ibrahim: 9].

Her saying "an old barren woman" is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "I am an old barren woman."

"'Ajuz" is fa'ul in the sense of fa'il, and it is the same for masculine and feminine; it is derived from 'ajz and is applied to advanced age because inability usually accompanies it.

"'Aqim" is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and it is the same for masculine and feminine when it agrees with a feminine noun; it is derived from 'aqamaha Allah, when He created her unable to bear a child. Sarah had never conceived.

The angels' saying "Thus has your Lord said" refers to the event, which is the announcement of a boy.

The kaf is for comparison, that is, like our saying: "Your Lord has said," so we have conveyed what we were commanded to convey.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing﴾ is a justification for the clause "Thus has your Lord said," which implies that the angels only informed Abraham as a conveyance from God, that God is truthful in His promise, that there is no room for the wonder of Abraham's wife, because God is Wise, who arranges the bringing into being of what He wills, and Knowing, to whom her state of infirmity and barrenness is not hidden.

This dialogue between the angels and Sarah, wife of Abraham, is similar to what occurred between them and Abraham, as recounted in Surah al-Hijr. So what passed between them and Sarah is related here, and what passed between them and Abraham is related there, while the setting is one and the situation is one, as explained in Surah Hud, where she said: ﴿O woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing!﴾ [Hud: 72].

Her saying "an old barren woman" is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "I am an old barren woman."
