Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing!﴾ [Hud: 72].

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verses 24–30:

﴿Has there come to you the story of Abraham's honored guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Peace, [you are] a people unknown [to me]."﴾ ﴿Then he turned quickly to his household and brought a fattened calf.﴾ ﴿And he set it before them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿So he felt within himself apprehension of them. They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a learned boy.﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry and struck her face and said, "[I am] an old barren woman!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus has your Lord said. Indeed, He is the Wise, the Knowing."﴾

This is a transition from warning, admonition and argument to taking lesson from the states of earlier nations that resemble the polytheists addressed in their disbelief and their denial of the messengers. The sentence is a fresh, independent beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i), and the style of speech shifts from direct address to the warners to an indirect style (ta'ridh), as a variation (tafannun) by mentioning the story of Abraham, to serve as a preface (tawti'ah) to the intended matter, which is the mention of what befell the people of Lot when they denied their messenger. Thus the intended point is what follows His saying: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 31].

Beginning with the mention of the people of Lot in this verse was contrary to the order that the Qur'an's usage followed in arranging the stories of the denying nations, which begin with the people of Noah, then 'Ad, then Thamud, then the people of Lot. The reason for the transition from the threat against the polytheists to the lesson of the earlier nations is that the polytheists were described just before as being "in heedlessness, neglectful" (ghamrah sahun), so in that heedlessness they were more akin to the people of Lot, of whom God said: ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication﴾ [al-Hijr: 72]. Also, the punishment with which the people of Lot were punished was stones sent down upon them from the sky, likened to rain. It was named "rain" in His saying: ﴿And they had certainly passed by the town which was rained upon with a rain of evil﴾ [al-Furqan: 40], and His saying: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74]. Moreover, in the story of the angels' presence with Abraham and his wife there is a lesson on the possibility of resurrection, for it includes the good tidings of a child who would be born to her after despair of childbearing; and that is like resurrection to life after death.

When the address was directed to the Prophet ﷺ with His saying "Has there come to you," it is understood that the primary purpose is to console him for what he met from his people's denial. Following from this is an indirect allusion to the hearers when the Qur'an is recited to them or he conveys to them that they are destined for a similar punishment, because the causes are the same.

The expression "Has there come to you" has already been discussed in the parallel at His saying: ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ [Sad: 21] in Surah Sad, and that such an expression introduces grand and important reports.

Al-dayf (the guest): a noun used for the singular and the plural, since its origin is the verbal noun of dhaafa, meaning "to incline," and it was applied to one who inclines toward someone's house to stay with him. Then it became a noun; when its origin is considered, it is applied to the singular and to others, and they do not make it feminine or plural; and when the noun itself is considered, they make it plural for groups and feminine for females, so they say adyaf and duyuf, and dayfah for a female guest. Here it is a collective noun (ism jam'), and therefore it is described by "the honored ones." It was discussed in Surah al-Hijr: ﴿He said, "Indeed, these are my guests"﴾ [al-Hijr: 68].

What is meant by them are the angels whom God made manifest to Abraham, peace be upon him, and who informed him that they were sent from God to carry out the punishment upon the people of Lot. God called them "guests" in view of the form of their coming in the appearance of guests, just as He called the two angels who came to Dawud "adversaries" in His saying: ﴿And has there come to you the news of the adversaries?﴾ [Sad: 21]; this is a formal metaphor (isti'arah suwariyyah).

In the Book of Genesis of the Torah, they were three. From Ibn 'Abbas: they were Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil. From 'Ata': Jibril, Mika'il, and with them another angel.

Perhaps the reason for sending three was that they would take the form of men, as people customarily know in their journeys that a caravan of travellers is not fewer than three companions. That is the origin of the address being in the dual form, as in: (qifa nabki). And in a hadith: "One is a devil, two are two devils, and three are a caravan." Narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, who said its chain is sahih.

It may also be that the reason for their being sent as three is that the punishment of the people of Lot was of different kinds, and each kind had its own angel assigned to it.

Describing them as "honored" is an oblique statement, for it gives the impression that this was for Abraham's honoring them, as was his custom with guests, and he was the one who established hospitality. The intended meaning is that God honored them by elevating their rank, for the angels are near to God, as He said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26], and He said: ﴿Noble writers﴾ [al-Infitar: 11].

The adverbial clause "when they entered upon him" is connected to "news" because it contains the sense of a verb, meaning: their report when they entered upon him.

His saying ﴿They said, "Peace," he said, "Peace"﴾ has a parallel discussed in Surah Hud. The majority read "qala salamun" (he said, "Peace"). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "qala silmun," with a kasrah on the sin and sukun on the lam.

His saying ﴿"[You are] a people unknown"﴾ is part of Abraham's speech. The apparent view is that he said it quietly, since it is not part of honoring a visitor to voice that openly to him. So the implied sense is: "They are a people unknown."

Al-munkar: one whose state is disliked by another, meaning not known. Here it is applied to one whose condition is unfamiliar and is thought to be an unusual state, that is, one feared to harbor evil, as He said in Surah Hud: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he found them strange and felt apprehension of them﴾ [Hud: 70]. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She disliked me, and what she disliked of the events was nothing but my grey hair and my baldness,"
meaning: she disliked my person.

The story of Abraham's guests has been discussed in Surah Hud.

"Raagha" means to incline sideways while walking, from which comes "rawaghan al-tha'lab" (the fox's dodging). The meaning is that Abraham turned aside from the place where the guests had alighted to his household, that is, to his house in which his family was.

In the Torah, he was sitting before the door of his tent under a tree, and he had brought the guests down beneath the tree.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam said: "raghan" is a deviation in walking from straightness toward a side while concealing that intention. Al-Raghib, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him in this restriction. From it al-Zamakhshari drew that Abraham's concealment of his inclination toward his household was part of good hospitality, so that he would not give the guest the impression that he intended to bring them something, lest the guest hold him back from that and excuse him. This is a subtle point.

The lodging of Abraham where this story took place was in a place called (Bulutat Mamra) in the land of Jabrun.

The calf is described here as "fattened" (samin), while in Surah Hud it is described as "roasted" (hanidh), that is, grilled; so it was a fattened calf which he grilled and set before them. Grilling was the quickest cooking of the desert people. Imru' al-Qays said, describing the hunt:

"So the cooks of meat stayed, between one who ripened the roast in slices and one who hastened the pot."

He restricted "pot" (qadir) with "hastened" (mu'ajjal), but did not restrict "slices of roast" (saffiyat shiwa'), because it is known.

The meaning of "qarrabahu" (he set it near them) is that he placed it close to them, that is, he did not move them from their seat to another place, but placed the food before them. This is part of completing honor for the guest, unlike what the one who seeks food or the beggar is given, for he is called to the place of the food, as al-Farazdaq said:

"I said, 'To the food,' and among them a group who envy the companionable one, the food."

The coming of the particle fa' to conjoin the verbs "fara'a," "fa-ja'a," "fa-qarrabahu" indicates that these actions happened swiftly, and hastening with hospitality is part of complete generosity, and it has been said: "The best of charity is that which is quickest."

The clause ﴿He said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ is a substitute clause (badal ishtimal) for the clause "he set it near them."

"Ala" is one word, and it is a particle of invitation (harf 'ard), that is, a desire for the act to take place that it precedes. Here it is definitely an invitation, because the verb of saying falls as a substitute for the verb "qarrabahu ilayhim," and it is not good to make it two words of interrogative hamzah for denial with the negative "la."

Offering food to the guest right after placing it before him is an increase in honor, by showing eagerness for what benefits the guest, even though placing the food before him is sufficient for enabling him to eat it. This has been considered by the jurists as permission for accepting invitations to banquets, as opposed to merely the existence of a table of food or a provision-cloth, since it may have been prepared for someone other than the invited guest.

The fa' in ﴿So he felt within himself apprehension of them﴾ is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasihah), because it discloses an implied sentence required by the connection of meaning, that is: "They did not eat, so he felt within himself apprehension of them," like His saying: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 63]. This was made explicit in Surah Hud: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾ [Hud: 70], that is, toward the calf, ﴿he found them strange and felt apprehension of them﴾ [Hud: 70].

(p. 5)

﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people,﴾ ﴿to send down upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ Ibrahim (Abraham) knew from their discourse, in what is mentioned in this verse and what is mentioned in other verses, that they were angels sent from Allah. So he asked them about the matter for which they had been sent. He asked them only after he had hosted them, in accordance with the custom of hospitality: a guest should not be asked about the purpose that brought him to the house until he is ready to depart, lest the host be suspected of weariness at his presence, and so that he may help him with his affair if he is able. Although they had given him good news of a great matter, he did not know whether that was the full extent of what they had come for.

The verb "said" (qala) is related without a conjunction, because its statements form a dialogue between him and his guest.

The fa (فَ) in what is related of Ibrahim's speech is the fa al-fasihah (the "eloquent fa," which signals an omitted clause). It indicates an omitted statement arising from the exchange between him and his guest. This is a case of a statement being conjoined to another speaker's statement. It occurs frequently with the conjunction wa (و), as in the words of the Most High, relating about Ibrahim, "He said, 'And of my offspring?'" after His words, "He said, 'Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people'" (al-Baqarah: 124), and His words relating about Nuh, "He said, 'And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?'" (al-Shu'ara': 112). So Ibrahim addressed the angels in his own language with what would be rendered by the eloquent Arabic phrase: "﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾"

The omitted part is estimated as: "Since you are messengers from the side of Allah the Exalted, what is your business for which you were sent?"

(p. 6)

Ibrahim knew that the descent of angels in that form would not be merely to give him good news of a son to be born to him and to his wife, since such good news came to him through revelation. So it was part of the knowledge of prophethood (ʿilm al-nubuwwah) that sending angels to the earth in that form would only be for a matter of importance. The Most High said, "We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be reprieved" (al-Hijr: 8).

Al-khatb (الخَطْب) means a great event and an important matter, and its attribution to their pronoun is due to the slightest connection.

The meaning is: "What is the matter for which you were sent, since the angels do not descend except with truth?" He addressed them with his words, "O messengers," because he did not know any other way to name them except by describing them as the messengers. The messengers are also among the attributes of angels, as in the words of the Most High, "By those sent forth in succession" (al-Mursalat: 1), according to one of the two interpretations.

By "the guilty people" is meant the people of Sodom (Sadum) and Gomorrah (ʿAmmuriyyah), who are the people of Lut (Lot). Their story has already been mentioned in Surat al-Aʿraf and Surat Hud.

The sending (irsal) in His words, "to send down upon them stones of clay," is used metaphorically for throwing, as one says, "He sent his arrow at the game." This sending occurs after the stones were lifted up into the air and then sent down upon them. For this reason they are called rain (matar) in some verses.

There is paronomasia (jinas) between arsalna (أرْسَلْنا) and linursila (لِنُرْسِلَ), because the meanings of the two words differ.

Al-hijarah (الحِجارَة) is a collective noun for al-hajar (stone). The meaning of the stones being of clay is that their origin is clay which became stone through the fire's melting. They are volcanic stones of sulfur, which the earth ejected from the place that became a lake now called the Dead Sea (Lake Lut), and a divine law (namus ilahi) lifted them up by pressure, which Allah made to raise what came out of the volcano into the air. They then descended upon the villages of Lut's people and destroyed them. This occurred by the command of creation through the mediation of angelic powers.

Al-musawwamah (المُسَوَّمَةُ) means that upon which there is a sumah, that is, a mark. That is, upon them were marks of colors indicating that they are not ordinary stones.

The meaning of "with your Lord" is that their marks were by the creation and formation of Allah.

(p. 7)

Al-musrifun (المُسْرِفُون) are those who exceed in disobedience, through their disbelief and the spread of immorality among them. So al-musrifun are the guilty people. He turned away from their pronoun to the apparent description, in order to record their excess in criminality.

(p. 5)

﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people,﴾ ﴿to send down upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ Ibrahim (Abraham) knew from their discourse, in what is mentioned in this verse and what is mentioned in other verses, that they were angels sent from Allah. So he asked them about the matter for which they had been sent. He asked them only after he had hosted them, in accordance with the custom of hospitality: a guest should not be asked about the purpose that brought him to the house until he is ready to depart, lest the host be suspected of weariness at his presence, and so that he may help him with his affair if he is able. Although they had given him good news of a great matter, he did not know whether that was the full extent of what they had come for.

The verb "said" (qala) is related without a conjunction, because its statements form a dialogue between him and his guest.

The fa (فَ) in what is related of Ibrahim's speech is the fa al-fasihah (the "eloquent fa," which signals an omitted clause). It indicates an omitted statement arising from the exchange between him and his guest. This is a case of a statement being conjoined to another speaker's statement. It occurs frequently with the conjunction wa (و), as in the words of the Most High, relating about Ibrahim, "He said, 'And of my offspring?'" after His words, "He said, 'Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people'" (al-Baqarah: 124), and His words relating about Nuh, "He said, 'And what knowledge do I have of what they used to do?'" (al-Shu'ara': 112). So Ibrahim addressed the angels in his own language with what would be rendered by the eloquent Arabic phrase: "﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾"

The omitted part is estimated as: "Since you are messengers from the side of Allah the Exalted, what is your business for which you were sent?"

(p. 6)

Ibrahim knew that the descent of angels in that form would not be merely to give him good news of a son to be born to him and to his wife, since such good news came to him through revelation. The Most High said, "We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be reprieved" (al-Hijr: 8).

Al-khatb (الخَطْب) means a great event and an important matter, and its attribution to their pronoun is due to the slightest connection.

The meaning is: "What is the matter for which you were sent, since the angels do not descend except with truth?" [Page 8]

This sentence is not part of the report of the angels' speech. Rather, it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the story of the dialogue between the angels and Ibrahim. The *fa'* in ﴿فَأخْرَجْنا﴾ is an explanatory *fa'* (fa' fasiha), because it reveals an implied statement, namely what is mentioned in Surah Hud about the angels' coming to Lut and what took place between him and his people. The implied meaning is: "They arrived at the town of Lut, and We commanded them to bring out those among its people who were believers, so they brought them out." The pronoun in ﴿أخْرَجْنا﴾ is the pronoun of majesty (the plural of greatness).

The attribution of the bringing out to Allah is because He commanded the angels to convey it to Lut, and because Allah facilitated the bringing out and the salvation of the believers by delaying the descent of the stones until the believers, namely Lut and his family except his wife, had gone out.

He referred to them as "the believers" to indicate that their faith was the cause of their salvation, that is, their faith in Lut. Referring to them as "the Muslims" is because they were the household of a prophet, and the faith of the prophets is submission (Islam). Allah said: ﴿And Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Ya'qub: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132].

The pronoun in ﴿فِيها﴾ refers back to the town, although no prior mention of it has been made, because it is known from other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town upon which rain of evil had been rained.﴾ [al-Furqan: 40].

The connection of ﴿فَما وجَدْنا﴾ is the connection of one report to another report. The verb *wajadna* here means "We knew," because *wajada* belongs to the sisters of *zanna* (verbs of mental perception). Its first object is the phrase ﴿مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾, and the *min* is *zā'ida* (superfluous, added for emphasis of the negation). The phrase ﴿فِيها﴾ is in the position of the second object.

[Page 9]

The reason He said ﴿فَأخْرَجْنا مَن كانَ فِيها مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ and ﴿فَما وجَدْنا فِيها غَيْرَ بَيْتٍ مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ﴾ rather than saying "We brought out Lut and the members of his household" is to draw attention to the status of faith and Islam; that is, Allah saved them from the punishment because of their faith in what their messenger had brought, not because they were the people of Lut. And the fact that they were the household of Lut is because the attribute of believers was confined to them in that town. So it was like a universal confined to one specific individual.

The *mu'min* is one who affirms what must be affirmed. The *muslim* is one who submits to the requirement of faith, and salvation is not achieved except by the combination of both matters. Thus there occurred in the statement, along with variety in the wording, an indication that both are to be honored, and that salvation lies in the combination of the two.

The verse indicates that the wife of Lut used to show submission to her husband while concealing disbelief and collusion with the people of the town in their corruption. Allah said: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10], and so on. So the household of Lut were all Muslims but not all of them were believers. Therefore, of them, only those who were characterized by both faith and Islam were saved.

The "finding" in His saying ﴿فَما وجَدْنا﴾ is intended to mean the connection of Allah's knowledge to the known thing after its occurrence, and this is a *tanjizi* connection (a connection of actual realization). The finding of a thing is its perception and attainment.

The meaning of ﴿وتَرَكْنا فِيها آيَةً﴾ is that the town remained in ruins and was not rebuilt, so what was in it of the traces of ruin was a sign for those who fear the punishment of Allah. Allah said in Surah Hud: "And indeed it is on a road that remains." Or the pronoun may refer to what is derived from the whole of His saying ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 32], by interpreting the speech as referring to the story; that is, "We left [a sign] in their story."

The literal meaning of *tark* (leaving) is the separation of a person from a thing that was with him in a place, so he departs from that place and leaves behind from it what was with him. As in the saying of Antarah:

*So I left him as prey for the beasts, which tug at him.*

It is also applied to causing a state to persist for a long time, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

*So do not leave me with threats, as if I were, among the people, a mangy camel smeared with tar.*

Here the persistence of that state is likened to a thing left in a place. The aspect of resemblance is the lack of change.

The *tark* in the verse is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for keeping a thing in a place without the leaver departing from it. Or it is a *majaz mursal* (figurative usage based on a loose relation) in this sense, so it is similar to what is in the verse of al-Nabigha.

Those who fear the punishment are the believers in the Resurrection and recompense, from among the people of Islam and the People of the Book, excluding the polytheists. For when they did not benefit from the indication of the sites of annihilation regarding the causes of that annihilation, the indication of its sign was treated, with respect to them, as the position of what is not a sign, as Allah said: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45].

The meaning is: those who fear took warning from the sign of the people of Lut and avoided the likes of the causes of their destruction, while those who associated partners with Allah do not take warning, so a painful punishment is about to descend upon them.

[Page 10]

His saying (﴿And in Moses﴾) is coordinated with his earlier statement "in them is a sign." The implied sense is: "And We left a sign in Moses." This is a coordination of one clause with another, with the verb "We left" (taraknā) supplied after the conjunctive wāw. The speech is elliptical, with an omitted noun, meaning: "in the story of Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority, and he turned away," and so on. The implied "leaving" in the particle of coordination is intended to make the indication remain, as though it were left in its place and not moved from it, as was mentioned just before in the verse of 'Antarah.

The story of Moses and Pharaoh follows the story of the people of Lot because of the fame of Moses' affair and his law. Thus the implied "leaving" is used in both its figurative senses: metonymy (majāz mursal) and metaphor (isti'ārah). In the wāw there is a use (istikhdām) similar to the use of a pronoun in the verse of Mu'awiya ibn Malik, known as Mu'awwid al-Hukamā' (the one who accustomed the wise). They gave him this title because of his saying, in mentioning his poem:

"I accustom the wise after me to its like, when truth has bitten in calamities. ***When the cloud descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

The meaning is that the story of Moses is a lasting sign.

The story of the people of Lot was followed by the story of Moses and Pharaoh because of the resemblance between them: the punishment with which both nations were punished was an earthly punishment. The people of Lot were punished with stones made of clay, and the people of Pharaoh were punished by drowning in the sea. Then 'Ad and Thamud were mentioned, and their punishment was from heaven: 'Ad were punished by a wind, and Thamud by a thunderbolt.

The "clear authority" (sultān mubīn) is the clear proof, namely the miracles that he showed to Pharaoh, such as the transformation of the staff into a serpent and the eight signs that followed it.

The primary meaning of "turning away" (tawallī) is departing from a place.

The primary meaning of "might" (rukn) is that on which one relies, such as a building or the like. The body is called a rukn because it is the pillar of a person's action.

His saying "he turned away with his might" is an analogy (tamthīl) depicting the manner of his rejection of Moses' call, in the form of one who turns away from a person. With the mention of "with his might," the analogy is complete; without it, "turned away" would be merely a metaphor.

The bā' here denotes accompaniment (mulābasah), meaning: accompanied by his might, as in the saying "he turned away and withdrew with his side."

The mulīm is one who causes others to blame him, meaning: he committed a sin for which God blames him, that is, holds him to account for it. The meaning is that he deserves punishment, as He said: ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

The meaning is that the story of Moses and Pharaoh is a sign for those who fear the painful punishment, so that they avoid the like of the causes of what befell Pharaoh and his people of punishment. These causes appeared in Pharaoh's arrogance in refusing to affirm the Messenger who was sent to him. And those who do not fear punishment do not believe in resurrection and recompense, and are not admonished by this, because they do not affirm the divine laws and do not reflect on the call of the people of truth. They continue to turn away, mocking the call of their Messenger, arrogant towards him and obstinate regarding the evidences of his truthfulness. So it is likely that there will befall them the like of what befell Pharaoh and his people, for what applies to the like applies to the one who resembles it. The Muslims used to say: "Abu Jahl is the Pharaoh of this community."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 41–42:

﴿And in ʿĀd, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ ﴿that left nothing it came upon without making it like rotted bones.﴾

The composition (naẓm) of this verse is like the composition of His saying ﴿And in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 38]. It moves on to the lesson drawn from one of the Arab nations, namely ʿĀd, who are the most famous of the extinct (bā'ida) Arabs.

The "barren wind" (al-rīḥ al-ʿaqīm) is the wind that is devoid of the benefits for which winds are hoped: stirring up and driving the clouds, and fertilizing trees by carrying the pollen (ghubra) of the male to the female trees. That is, it is the wind in which there is no benefit, i.e., it is harmful. This description, being derived from something that is among the characteristics of females, did not need the attachment of the feminine marker (hāʾ al-taʾnīth), because that marker is brought in to distinguish between the two categories. The Arabs dislike barrenness (ʿuqm) in their livestock; so the wind is like a barren she-camel that produces neither offspring nor milk. Describing the wind as ʿaqīm is therefore an eloquent metaphor for ill omen. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Or there came upon them the punishment of a barren day﴾ [al-Hajj: 55].

The clause ﴿that left nothing it came upon without making it like rotted bones﴾ is a second attribute, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is an escalation in the harm of this wind, for it gives no benefit, and it causes tremendous harm.

The verb "tadharu" is in the present form to make the strange situation present to the mind.

"Shay'" (thing) functions in the sense of the object of "tadharu"; (min) here is for emphasizing the negation, and the indefinite noun governed by min is explicit in negating the genus, which is why it is general. However, this generality is specified by rational evidence, because the wind only wears away things over which it passes when they are by nature susceptible to decay. The wind does not wear away mountains, seas or valleys, even though it passes over them; it wears away only dwellings, trees, people and animals. A similar example is His saying: ﴿It destroys everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25].

The clause "jaʿalathu ka-l-ramīm" (it made it like rotted bones) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the wind. It is an exception from the generality of the states of "shay'," clarifying what is defined: that is, "it left nothing it came upon, in any of the states of its destruction, except in a state in which it had made it like rotted bones."

"Al-ramīm" means the bone that has decayed. It is said: "ramma al-ʿaẓm" when the bone decayed, that is, it made it crumbled.

The meaning: and in ʿĀd there is a sign for those who fear the painful punishment, when God sent the wind upon them. The intended point is that the sign lies in the causes of God's sending the wind upon them, and these causes were their denial of Hud and their associating partners with God, and their saying: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" So whoever believes should beware of a fate like that which befell them. As for those among the people of polytheism who do not fear the painful punishment, they persist in their disbelief just as ʿĀd persisted; so it is likely that there will befall them something of the same kind as what befell ʿĀd.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 43–45:

﴿And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ ﴿But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on.﴾ ﴿And they were not able to stand up [against it], nor were they among those who could defend themselves.﴾

The story of 'Ad was followed by the story of Thamud because the two are frequently mentioned together in the Qur'an, since Thamud was contemporary with 'Ad and succeeded them in the greatness of nations, as Allah says: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ [al-A'raf: 74], and because both were well known among the Arabs.

﴿And in Thamud﴾ is a conjunction with "in 'Ad" or with "We left in it a sign."

The meaning is: We left a sign for the believers in Thamud, in a state in which the thunderbolt seized them, i.e., in the indication of the seizing of the thunderbolt upon them, that its cause was their polytheism, their denial, and their defiance of the command of their Lord. So the believers took warning from that and followed the path of salvation from its consequences, while the polytheists, by persisting in their disbelief, would bring upon themselves a punishment of the same kind as that which befell Thamud.

This statement mentioned here is a comprehensive saying encompassing what their prophet Salih warned them of and reminded them of, such as his saying ﴿And He settled you in the land, you take from its plains palaces and carve out the mountains as houses﴾ [al-A'raf: 74]

صفحة ١٣
and his saying ﴿Will you be left in what is here, secure?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 146] ﴿in gardens and springs﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 15] ﴿and crops and palm trees with their spathes tender﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 148], and his saying ﴿He it is who produced you from the earth and made you inhabit it﴾ [Hud: 61]. And the like of that, which indicates that they were given what is enjoyment (mata'), i.e., benefit in this world, for the benefits of this world are fleeting. So the words that their prophet spoke were a reminder of Allah's blessing upon them, gathered in "Enjoy yourselves for a time," although it is possible that their prophet said this comprehensive phrase to them and it is not related in the Qur'an except in this place, for you have learned from the seventh introduction of this exegesis that the reports of nations come dispersed across their stories in the Qur'an.

So His saying "Enjoy yourselves" (tamatta'u) is used to mean permission to enjoy. Mata' has been made to mean blessing in many places, such as His saying ﴿And the life of this world in the Hereafter is nothing but mata'﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], and His saying ﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you and a mata' for a time﴾ [al-Anbiya': 111].

What is meant by "ḥīn" is an indefinite period, made the end of the blessings they were given to enjoy, for the blessings of this world are fleeting. That term is either the appointed time of each one of them, at which his life ends, or the appointed time of the nation, at which its survival ends.

This is like His saying ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision until an appointed term﴾ [Hud: 3]. Just as Allah said to people through the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ, He perhaps said it to Thamud through the tongue of Salih (peace be upon him).

His saying ﴿when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time"﴾ does not point to His saying in another verse ﴿So they hamstrung her, and he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your home for three days"﴾ [Hud: 65] and the like, because that command is used for warning and for despairing them of salvation after three days; so His subsequent saying "but they defied the command of their Lord" has no fitting connection to it with the fa' (then) particle, because what the fa' indicates requires that what follows it be ordered in existence after what precedes it.

"'Utuww" means arrogance and severity. "'Ataw" is construed with the sense of "turned away," so it takes "'an" (from), i.e., they turned away from what Allah commanded them through the tongue of His messenger Salih (peace be upon him).

The seizing of the thunderbolt (akhdh al-sa'iqa) of them means its striking them with a strike resembling the way an enemy seizes his enemy.

The clause "while they were looking on" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of object in "akhadhnahum," i.e., We seized them

صفحة ١٤
while they were looking at its descent; for when they saw its fierce flashes, they knew that it was not customary, so they stood up looking at the clouds, and the thunderbolt descended upon them while they were looking. That is a great terror, an increase in the punishment, for looking at the retribution increases its sufferer's pain, just as looking at a blessing increases the one blessed's joy. Allah says ﴿And We drowned the family of Pharaoh while you were looking on﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50].
Al-Kisa'i read (al-sa'qa) without an alif.

His saying ﴿So they were not able to stand up [against it]﴾ is a consequence of "while they were looking on," i.e., they were unable to repel that at the moment they saw its harbingers. "Qiyam" here is a metaphor for defense, as one says: "This is a matter no one can stand against," i.e., no one can repel it. In a hadith: "He became angry with an anger no one could stand against," i.e., they were not able to make any defense against that.

His saying "nor were they among those who could defend themselves" means: He did not help them so that they could be ones who defend themselves, because "intaṣara" is the reflexive (muṭāwi') of "naṣara," i.e., no one helped them so that they defended themselves.

His saying "nor were they among those who could defend themselves" means: He did not help them so that they could be ones who defend themselves, because "intaṣara" is the reflexive (muṭāwi') of "naṣara," i.e., no one helped them so that they defended themselves.

﴿And the people of Nuh before them. Indeed, they were a people who were defiant.﴾ The majority of reciters read "wa-qawma" (وقَوْمَ) in the accusative, by supposing an implied "remember" (اذْكُرْ) or an implied verb indicated by the narratives mentioned before it. Its sense is: "And We destroyed the people of Nuh." This is coordination of clauses (عطف الجمل) and not coordination of single words (عطف المفردات).

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it in the genitive (بِالجَرِّ), coordinating it with "Thamud," on the supposition: "And in the people of Nuh."

The meaning of "min qabl" (مِن قَبْلُ) is that they were destroyed before those (peoples). Thus they were the first of the nations that denied their messenger and were destroyed.

The clause "Indeed, they were a people who were defiant" (إنَّهم كانُوا قَوْمًا فاسِقِينَ) gives the reason for what is contained in His saying "And the people of Nuh before them." The sense of their being a sign for those who fear the punishment is: from the fact that they were punished, and that their punishment was because they were a people who were defiant.

[Page 15]

He postponed the discussion of the people of Nuh because of the conflicting considerations (تَجاذُبِ المُناسَباتِ) that arose in what was presented of the signs of punishment for the nations mentioned just before, as you already know. For this reason his saying "min qabl" is an alert to the reason for departing from the Qur'an's usual order in narrating the conditions of nations according to their order of existence.

His saying "min qabl" has already pointed to this, and similar to it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾ [al-Najm: 50], ﴿and Thamud, and spared none﴾ [al-Najm: 51], ﴿and the people of Nuh before them. Indeed, they were more unjust and more tyrannical﴾ [al-Najm: 52].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 47:

﴿And the heaven We constructed with power, and indeed We are expanding [it].﴾

Since the doubt of those who deny the Resurrection rested on the supposed impossibility of restoring bodies after they have perished, the verse follows their threat with something that dispels that supposition. The address is directed to them, reminding them that God created the greatest of creations when it was not a thing at all. Thus the restoration of perishable things, in comparison with it, is only a trivial matter, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir: 57].

This sentence and the sentences conjoined to it, up to His saying "Indeed I am to you a clear warner" [cf. 51:50], are parenthetical, placed between the clause "﴿And [the people of] Noah before, [they were a people who defied]﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 46]" etc., and the clause ﴿Thus did there not come to those before them any messenger﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52] and what follows.

The creation began with the heaven because the heaven is the greatest created thing that people observe. The creation of the earth is conjoined to it as the conjunction of a thing with its opposite, because opposites are associated in the imaginative faculty. The creation of the kinds of animals is conjoined to these because they are near to sight; contemplating them and reflecting on their conditions does not burden the minds as much.

The verb "building" is used figuratively for the creation of the heaven, because the appearance of the heaven to sight resembles a dome, and the erecting of a dome is called building.

This is an argument from the effect of a creation whose effect they witnessed though they did not witness its manner, because its effect indicates the greatness of its manner, and that it is greater than what is conceivable regarding the manner of restoring decayed bodies.

"Al-Ayd" means power. Its origin is the plural of "yad" (hand), then its usage became widespread until it became a name for power. It was discussed earlier at His saying "﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength﴾ [Sad: 17]" in Surat Sad.

The meaning: We built it with a power that no one is able to match.

The placing of "the heaven" before its governing verb is for emphasis on it. Then, by using the construction of "al-ishtighal" (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the object), it is further strengthened so that the object is connected to its verb twice: once by itself and once by its pronoun, since the construction of ishtighal is in the force of repeating the clause. Its emphasis is further increased by concluding with His saying "﴿And indeed We are expanding [it]﴾", and the waw is parenthetical.

"Al-Muwsi'" is the active participle of "awsa'," meaning one who possesses "wus'," i.e., power. Its derivatives come from "al-sa'a" (spaciousness), which is the extension of the extent of a place, the opposite of narrowness. Its meaning is figuratively used for abundance in things such as individuality, like its generality in ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], and the abundance of wealth, like ﴿Let one of wide means spend from his means﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], and His saying "and upon the one of means is his due measure." Among His names, the Most Expansive (al-Wasi') occurs: ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. When it is applied to the Essence, it indicates the perfection of His essential attributes: existence, life, knowledge, power, and wisdom, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115]. From this is His saying here: ﴿And indeed We are expanding [it]﴾.

He emphasized the statement with the particle "inna" to treat the addressees as one who denies the vastness of God's power, since they deemed the restoration of created things after their decay to be impossible.

**[p. 17]**

The discussion of placing "the earth" (al-ard) before its governing verb, and of the construction of the verb with a pronoun (ishtighal), is the same as the discussion of "﴿wal-samā'a banaynāhā﴾" ("And the sky, We built it"). The same applies to using this as evidence for the possibility of resurrection.

Among the subtleties of Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi): the mention of the four peoples points to the fact that God punished them through the very things that are the causes of their existence, namely earth, water, air and fire, which are the elements of existence. He destroyed the people of Lot with stones, and stones are made of clay. He destroyed the people of Pharaoh with water. He destroyed 'Ad with wind, which is air. He destroyed Thamud with fire.

Ibn 'Ashur adds that he dispensed here with repeating "bi-aydin" (with power), because what precedes it indicates it.

Al-farsh (spreading) is the spreading of a garment or the like for sitting or lying down. In "farashnāhā" there is an *istiʻāra tabaʻiyya* (a dependent metaphor, i.e. a metaphor in a verb or derivative): God's bringing the earth into being in a state of extension is likened to the spreading of a carpet or the like.

In this spreading there is a proof of God's power and wisdom, since He made the earth extended when He willed to place upon its surface kinds of animals that walk upon it, recline on it and lie down on it. Had it not been so, it would have been humped, hurting the walker, let alone the one who reclines or lies down.

Since there was in its spreading a purpose, He made it a cradle (mahd) for whoever is on it of mankind. He followed "farashnāhā" with a consequent praise of Himself for perfecting its preparation, as a reminder of His greatness and bounty. That is: ﴿so how excellent are the spreaders!﴾, meaning "We."

The plural form in His saying "al-māhidūn" (the spreaders) is for magnification, like the plural pronoun in "lillāh" (for God). In describing the creation of the earth, what appears to people of its surface was taken into account, because that is what matters to people in drawing evidence for God's power and in acknowledging His favour toward them through what is in His gentleness and kindness to them, without touching on its being spherical, since they cannot grasp it. Likewise, in mentioning the sky, what appears of the dome of its atmosphere was taken into account, without inquiry into the vast extent of its edges or the multiplicity of its worlds, which is beyond this purpose. For this reason he followed the parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) with the concluding phrase (tadhyīl) "﴿so how excellent are the spreaders!﴾". Its purpose is to teach people to praise God for what He has done for them in it of bounty, so that they may thank Him with that praise, as in His saying: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Zumar: 75].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 49:

﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember.﴾ When His saying ﴿So We spread it out, and how excellent are the Spreaders﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 48] indicated that in that there is a blessing upon the existing things that are on the earth, He followed that with the attribute of the creation of those existing things, because of what it contains of indication of God the Exalted's singularity in creation, which entails His singularity in divinity. So He said, ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾. And the zawj (pair) is the male and the female. And what is meant by "thing" is the kind within the class of animals. And the dual form of zawj here is because what is intended by it is that which is paired, male and female.

This argument against them is by means of a creation whose modes and stages they witness whenever they turn their eyes and strike their minds, namely the creation of male and female, so that from the two there may come about the bringing into being of a new creation that succeeds what preceded it. This is the closest illustration of the bringing forth of creation after annihilation, which is the resurrection that they denied, because things are brought closer to understanding by what is clear of the conditions of their likes.

Therefore He followed it with His saying ﴿that you may remember﴾, i.e., that you may reflect upon the differences between the possible and the impossible, and reflect upon the levels of possibility, so that the improbability and the scarcity of familiarity do not get mixed up for you with impossibility, such that you imagine the strange to be impossible.

So "remembering" is used in the customary sense of reflecting upon things and reviewing their own selves regarding what they have deemed impossible, so that after re-examining they would know that what they deemed impossible is possible, but they were not accustomed to it, so the strange became confused with the impossible for them, and so they deemed it impossible. Since renewing reflection on what has been neglected resembles remembering a forgotten thing, He applied to it ﴿that you may remember﴾. This is in the sense of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We are not outstripped from replacing your likenesses and bringing you into being in what you do not know. And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 60–62]. There it was concluded with urging remembrance, just as here it was concluded with hope of remembrance, which conveys that the creation of male and female from a drop is the first creation, and that it is the indication of the final creation.

The clause ﴿that you may remember﴾ is a causal clause for the clause ﴿We created pairs﴾, i.e., in hope that there may be in the two spouses a remembrance for you, i.e., an indication that has been neglected.

The discussion of the hope's issuing from God is clarified by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you may give thanks﴾ [al-Baqara: 52] in Surat al-Baqara.

After having clarified the error of these people in denying the Resurrection with a clear proof, and having likened their state to that of the earlier nations who denied the messengers and what they brought, combining admonition for the astray with consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, and what preceded was an indication that Allah alone creates the world, and in that is the refutation of their associating other gods with Allah, he turned to instructing the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he should derive for them after that, by calling them to return to the truth with His saying ﴿So flee to Allah﴾.

The clause introduced by the *fa'* (the particle "so") is the answer to an omitted saying, and the estimate is: "So say, 'Flee!'" This is indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner﴾, for it is a statement that issues only from a speaker, and it is not proper that it be the statement of a mere conveyor.

The omission of "say" is very frequent in the Qur'an and is one of the forms of its concision. The *fa'* belongs to the speech that the Messenger (ﷺ) utters, and its function is to derive a conclusion from what has been established previously. It does not derive from the omitted imperative verb, because what is derived by *fa'* is what is mentioned after it.

The style has been changed from admonition to addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he would deliver this admonition to them, because the multiplicity of those who admonish has an effect on the souls of those being addressed.

The more fitting reading in context is that "fleeing to Allah" is a metaphor (*isti'ara*) for abandoning the associationism in which they are. The denial of the Resurrection is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*, a metaphor in which a whole scene is depicted), by likening the state of their being entangled in error to the state of one who is in a dangerous place, whose condition calls him to flee from it to someone who will grant him protection. And the state of the Messenger (ﷺ) is likened to the state of a warner to a people that their homes are exposed to the raid of an enemy. So the compound expression "flee to Allah" is used in this depiction.

Thus, those addressed by "flee to Allah" are the polytheists, because the believers have already fled to Allah from polytheism.

*Al-firar* (fleeing) is running away, that is, the swift departure from a place to avoid a harm that would befall one there. It is construed with *min* of origin for the place where the harm is, as is said: "He fled from the land of the plague," and "from death," and with the thing that harms, as is said: "He fled from the lion," and "he fled from the enemy."

The clause "Indeed, I am to you from Him a clear warner" is a justification for the command "flee to Allah," on the basis that the purpose of warning is seeking safety from punishment; so the warning, in this respect, becomes a justification for the command to flee to Allah, that is, turning towards Him alone.

[p. 20]

His saying "from Him" (*minhu*) is an attribute of "warner," placed before the noun it qualifies, so it becomes a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The letter *min* here is for the figurative origin (*li-l-ibtida' al-majazi*), meaning: "one commanded by Him to deliver to you."

The conjunction of "and do not make with Allah another god" to "so flee to Allah" is a prohibition against attributing divinity to anyone other than Allah.

He combined the command and the prohibition for emphasis in affirmation, by negating the opposite in order to establish its contrary, as in His saying ﴿Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 79].

Among the subtle points of Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner﴾ includes the Messenger, those to whom he was sent, and the One who sent him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 52:

﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾

The word *kadhalika* ("thus") is *fasl al-khitab* (a decisive particle that marks the end of one discourse and the beginning of another, or a return to an earlier discourse which the later discourse had interrupted). The implied meaning is: "The matter is thus," with the demonstrative referring to what has preceded in the discourse. Then another discourse is introduced after it, and the listener relates each part to what fits it. Thus what follows the demonstrative is connected to the reports of the nations mentioned earlier, from the people of Lut and those joined with them.

The threat against the polytheists, that there would befall them what befell the nations who denied the messengers of Allah before them, is followed by a comparison of them with those nations in their saying. The word *kadhalika* has already occurred as a decisive particle in the words of Allah, ﴿Thus; and We encompassed what was with him in knowledge﴾ [al-Kahf: 91], in Surah al-Kahf. So His saying *kadhalika* is a decisive particle, and the clause ﴿what came to those before them of a messenger﴾ up to the end of the verse is a resumptive clause of initial resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*).

It is also possible to take His saying, ﴿Thus, what came to those before them﴾ to its end, as the beginning of a new resumption, or as a return to the condemnation of the polytheists for their statement, which varies in kinds of denial regarding tawhid, resurrection, and what branches from these. 

[Page 21]

The demonstrative refers to His saying, ﴿Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 8], up to the end of the verse, as you know from that place. That is: like their contradictory saying, those before them said when the messengers came to them. In this case, His saying *kadhalika* is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), and the one it refers to is "those before them."

On both readings, the meaning is that the state of these people is like the state of those who preceded them, from among those who were polytheists, in describing the Messenger ﷺ as a sorcerer or a madman. Thus these people too will answer your saying, "Flee to Allah, and do not set up with Allah another god," with the same kind of answer given by those before them. So there is no hope that they will turn back from their obstinacy.

By ﴿those before them﴾ [al-Zumar: 50] is meant the nations mentioned in the preceding verses and others. The pronoun in *qablihim* refers to the present polytheists of the Arabs.

The addition of *min* in His saying ﴿a messenger﴾ is to make explicit that the generality is intended: that every messenger was said of by a group from his people, "He is a sorcerer or a madman." That is, some of them said, "A sorcerer," and some of them said, "A madman," as with the people of Nuh, who did not say "sorcerer," since sorcery was not known in their time. They said, ﴿He is only a man possessed by madness, so wait for him for a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 25]. And sometimes they combined the two sayings, as with the saying of Pharaoh about Musa.

This generality indicates that no people among the mentioned nations was free of saying to its messenger one of the two sayings. What is reported of some of them in other verses, in the same wording or its synonym, is like the saying of the people of Hud, ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾ [Hud: 54].

The first of the messengers is Nuh, as is explicit in the sound hadith concerning intercession (*shafa'ah*). So it is not objected that Adam was not denied by his family, or that the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Joshua and Isaiah, were not denied by their people. This is because Allah said ﴿a messenger﴾, and the messenger is more specific than the prophet.

The exception in ﴿but they said, "A sorcerer"﴾ is an exception from omitted states. The meaning is: ﴿what came to those before them of a messenger﴾ in any state of their sayings, except in the state of their saying, "A sorcerer or a madman."

[Page 22]

The restriction (*qasr*) derived from the exception is an ostensive restriction (*qasr idda'i*), because those nations had other sayings and other states. They restricted themselves to this only out of concern to mention this strange state of slander, since they accuse the most intelligent of people of madness and the most upright of them of sorcery.

The attribution of the saying to the pronoun of "those before" the present polytheists of the Arabs is an attribution based on the fact that it is the saying of most of them, since matters attributed to nations and tribes proceed on the basis of what is most prevalent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 53:

﴿Did they bequeath it to one another? Nay, they are a people who are transgressors.﴾

The interrogative is used to express wonder at their agreement upon this saying, in the manner of an eloquent metaphor (al-tashbih al-baligh), i.e., as if some of them had enjoined on others that they should say it.

The interrogative here is a kinayah (metonymy) for its implication, which is wonder, because the nature of a wondrous matter is that one asks about it. The sentence is a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because the similarity of these nations in the saying of denial prompts the question of a questioner about the source of this resemblance.

The pronoun in "tawasaw" (they enjoined one another) refers back to what preceded of the relative pronoun and of the pronoun that was made its annex, "qablihim" (before them), i.e., some of them enjoined others, until the injunction reached the people present.

The pronoun in "bihi" (by it) refers to the verbal noun derived from the verb in "﴿illa qalu sahirun aw majnun﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52]", i.e., did they enjoin one another with this saying?

The verb of enjoining (wasiyyah) is transitive to the one enjoined by the preposition "ba'" (bi), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa tawasaw bil-haqqi wa tawasaw bis-sabr﴾ [al-'Asr: 3].

"Bal" (nay, rather) is a turning away (idrab) from what the interrogative implies, either from the resemblance or from the mutual enjoining about it, by explaining the cause of the agreement upon this saying, for when the cause becomes apparent, the wonder is dispelled. That is: it is not a mutual enjoining, but rather a similarity in the source of that saying, i.e., the cause of the similarity of the saying is the similarity of thinking and the motives for the saying;

page 23

since all of them are a people who are transgressors, and their tyranny and arrogance prevent them from following a Messenger whom they reckon themselves greater than. And since they find no defect with which to brand him, they invented, to belittle him, pretexts that do not fall under proof, namely the claim that he is a madman or that he is a sorcerer; so they were equal in that, by the cause of their equality in its causes and meanings.
Thus the pronoun in "hum qawmun taghun" (they are a people who are transgressors) refers to what the pronoun in "atawasaw" referred to.

And in the insertion of the word "qawm" (people) is an indication that transgression is firmly rooted in their souls, to the extent that it is among the constituents of their peoplehood, as was previously mentioned in His saying, ﴿la-ayatin li-qawmin ya'qiluna﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Dhariyat (51), verses 54–55:**

﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed.﴾ ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers.﴾

This is a consequence of His saying ﴿Thus did no messenger come to those before them, except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52] up to His saying "﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾" [al-Dhariyat: 53]. It implies that they are far from being persuaded by the signs and warnings, so ﴿turn away from them﴾, that is, stop insisting in arguing with them. The Prophet ﷺ was very eager for their faith and grieved over their obstinacy in disbelief, so God would repeatedly console him from time to time, as He said: ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief that they do not believe.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3] ﴿So perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this message.﴾ [al-Kahf: 6] ﴿And do not grieve over them, nor be distressed by what they plot.﴾ [al-Naml: 70]. So "turning away" is meant in this sense. Otherwise, the Qur'an came after verses like this one, calling them and arguing with them more than once. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So turn away from them for a time, and watch them, for they will [soon] see.﴾ [al-Saffat: 174], in Surah al-Saffat.

After His command to turn away from them, He informed him that there is no blame on him for their turning away from him. The statement is phrased as a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun) rather than "we do not blame you," to indicate the permanence of the content of the sentence in negation.

The second person pronoun is used as the subject, saying ﴿fa-ma anta bi-malum﴾ ("you are not to be blamed") rather than saying "fa-la" ("so there is no") "blame upon you" or something similar, for the purpose of attention, to honour the addressee and to exalt his status.

The particle "bi" (ب) is added to the negated predicate to emphasise the negation of his being blameworthy.

The conjunction of "wa-dhakkir" (وذَكِّرْ) to "﴿fa-tawalla 'anhum﴾" is a precaution, lest anyone should imagine that turning away nullifies the reminding; rather, the reminding remains. The Prophet ﷺ indeed reminded people after verses like these, and some who had not believed before then believed. Continuing the reminder is also an increase in establishing proof against those who turn away, and so that they do not increase in transgression, saying: "Here we are, we have silenced him," and so he stops what he is saying.

The command in "wa-dhakkir" is meant to express perpetual continuation of reminding and renewing it.

In justifying the command to remind, only one reason is mentioned, namely the benefit of the reminder to the believers, because the benefit of this is certain. It also shows care for the believers in a context where indifference to the disbelievers is displayed. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits. He who fears will be reminded, and the most wretched will avoid it.﴾ [al-A'la: 9].

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Dhariyat (51), verses 54–55:**

﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed.﴾ ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers.﴾

This is a consequence of His saying ﴿Thus did no messenger come to those before them, except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52] up to His saying "﴿Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾" [al-Dhariyat: 53]. It implies that they are far from being persuaded by the signs and warnings, so ﴿turn away from them﴾, that is, stop insisting in arguing with them. The Prophet ﷺ was very eager for their faith and grieved over their obstinacy in disbelief, so God would repeatedly console him from time to time, as He said: ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief that they do not believe.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3] ﴿So perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this message.﴾ [al-Kahf: 6] ﴿And do not grieve over them, nor be distressed by what they plot.﴾ [al-Naml: 70]. So "turning away" is meant in this sense. Otherwise, the Qur'an came after verses like this one, calling them and arguing with them more than once. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So turn away from them for a time, and watch them, for they will [soon] see.﴾ [al-Saffat: 174], in Surah al-Saffat.

The statement is phrased as a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun) rather than "we do not blame you," to indicate the permanence of the content of the sentence in negation.

The particle "bi" (ب) is added to the negated predicate to emphasise the negation of his being blameworthy.

The Prophet ﷺ indeed reminded people after verses like these, and some who had not believed before then believed. Continuing the reminder is also an increase in establishing proof against those who turn away, and so that they do not increase in transgression, saying: "Here we are, we have silenced him," and so he stops what he is saying.

The command in "wa-dhakkir" is meant to express perpetual continuation of reminding and renewing it.

[Page 25]

The more apparent view is that this verse is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the statement ﴿Thus did no messenger come to those before them﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:52] and what follows it, which arises from the phrase "So flee to Allah" through to ﴿And do not set up with Allah another god﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:51].

This is the conjoining of one purpose to another purpose, because of the connection between them. After He had compared their state with the state of the nations that persisted in denial before them, He followed it with a mention of the reprehensible state of their deviation from that for which they were created and in which they were disposed.

So His saying ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ is a declarative statement used as an allusion (ta'ridh) directed at the polytheists, who deviated from the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which they were created, opposing its established way (sunnah), following the misguidance of those who misguide.

Al-jinn: a kind of created beings hidden from people's eyes. It is a genus that includes the devils (shayatin). Allah the Exalted said of Iblis, "He was of the jinn" [al-Kahf 18:50].

Al-ins: a collective noun whose singular is insi, with the relative ya (ya' al-nisbah) attached to its plural.

The intended subject of this statement is mankind, and the jinn are mentioned only by way of incorporation (idmaj). You will learn the reason for this.

The exception (istithna') here is an "emptied" exception (mufarragh), omitting general causes, following the manner of the emptied exception.

The lam in "liya'budun" is the lam of cause, meaning: I did not create them for any cause except the cause of their worship of Me. The implied sense is: "for My desire that they worship Me." This is indicated by His saying in the explanatory clause, ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me﴾.

This interpretation applies to every lam that occurs in the Qur'an as the cause of an act of Allah the Exalted. That is, I am not pleased that they exist except that they acknowledge to Me the sole right to divinity.

Thus the meaning of "will" (irada) here is approval (rida) and love (mahabbah). It is not the divine attribute by which the possible is specified with some of what is permissible for it in accordance with knowledge, the attribute from which His name "the Willer" (al-Murid) is derived. For applying "will" to that is another usage, so the intent here is not to explain the actions of creatures that arise from their acquisition (kasb), according to the terminology of the Ash'arites, or from their power, according to the terminology of the Mu'tazilites, despite the closeness between the two terminologies. This is because it is evident that the actions of creatures may contradict the will of Allah concerning them in the sense of the attribute of will.

Allah created people [with a constitution] that calls for reflection upon the existence of God and leads to His unity. But the acquisition of people diverts their actions from the clear path for which they were created. The causes that enable them to deviate are numerous and go back to the intertwining of motives, actions, instruments and obstacles.

[Page 26]

This makes unnecessary several possible interpretations of the causal clause "liya'budun": (1) making the generality of the jinn and mankind restricted to the believers among them; (2) positing an omitted element in the speech, meaning "except that I command them to worship Me"; or (3) understanding worship in the sense of humble submission and supplication, which none of them is free from in times of need, such as sickness or drought. Ibn 'Atiyyah also mentioned this.

Against all those possibilities, it is objected that many of mankind do not worship, as is evident by observation, and that Allah related of some of the jinn that they do not worship.

We say: Allah created many creatures and placed within them an order and laws (nawamis). So each creature moves by what the laws of its natural constitution impel it to. Some creatures may harm others by undoing what was prepared for them, and some may harm others by undoing what they seek. Thus the states and laws of creatures become intertwined. Sometimes they support and reinforce one another, and sometimes they contradict and repel one another. From this arise states that cannot be counted, cannot be fully grasped, nor their paths or outcomes comprehended. Often these states result in the opposite of what the creature was prepared for in its original nature. For this reason Allah surrounded them with the laws of the sacred law (shara'i'), that is, a contradiction arose between the cosmic command (al-amr al-takwini) and the legislative command (al-amr al-tashri'i).

The meaning of worship (ibadah) in the Arabic language before the emergence of the technical religious terms has a subtle semantic range, and the statements of the linguistic authorities concerning it are unclear. What is extracted from them is that it is the manifestation of submission to the one worshipped, together with the belief that he possesses the benefit and harm of the worshipper in an intrinsic, continuous ownership. Thus the one worshipped is a god (ilah) to the worshipper, as Allah related the statement of Pharaoh: ﴿And their people are servants to us﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:47].

The restriction (qasr) derived from His saying ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ is the restriction of the cause of Allah's creation of mankind and the jinn to His will that they worship Him. The apparent view is that it is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), of the type of restricting the described to the description, and that it is a restriction by reversal (qasr qalb) with respect to the object of "yaʿbudun," meaning: "except that they worship Me alone." That is, not that they associate others with Me in worship. So it is a rejection of association (shirk), and it is not an absolute restriction. For although we do not know the measures of Allah the Exalted's wisdom in creating the creatures,

[Page 27]

we know that the wisdom behind their creation is not merely that they worship Him, because Allah's wisdoms in His acts are many and we cannot encompass them. Mentioning some of them, as here, does not imply that no other wisdom exists. Do you not see that Allah mentioned other wisdoms for creation, such as His saying ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud 11:118–119], not to mention what He mentioned of the wisdom in creating some of mankind and the jinn, such as His saying about the creation of Jesus, ﴿And that We may make him a sign for mankind and a mercy from Us﴾ [Maryam 19:21].

Furthermore, the acknowledgment of the creatures to the oneness of Allah dispels their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), because they only denied him because he called them to renounce association, which they claimed no one could renounce. So when their denial is dispelled, the dispelling of it entails the carrying out of the laws that the Messenger (ﷺ) brings, if they believe in Allah alone and obey what the Messenger (ﷺ) conveyed to them from Him. This is a meaning required by the worship of Allah by implication (dilalat al-iltizam). This is what is called worship in the absolute sense, the term used in the Sunnah in such sayings as his (ﷺ) words "that you worship Allah as if you see Him." It does not befit this to be the intended meaning in this verse, because it does not consistently serve as the cause for the creation of mankind. Legal obligations appear in some nations and some eras, and lapse in the periods of gaps between messengers until Islam came. I believe that applying the term worship to this meaning is a technical religious usage, even though the Qur'an did not use it in this sense, but it occurs frequently in the Sunnah and became commonly known among the Muslim community from the time Islam emerged.

Moreover, Allah's obligations for the servants, conveyed through the tongues of the messengers, were intended only for their immediate and eventual welfare and for the attainment of spiritual perfection through that welfare. Therefore Allah undoubtedly intended from the sacred laws the perfection of humanity and the regulation of its social order across its various eras. That is the wisdom of His creating. So His saying "except that they should worship Me" entails that He created them only so that their affairs would be ordered by their stopping at the limits of the legislative obligations, of commands and prohibitions. Thus a person's worship of his Lord is nothing other than an act that accomplishes the purpose of his creation and a usual cause for its attainment.

It is related from Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam that the interpretation of His saying ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ is: "except that I should command them and forbid them." Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi followed this interpretation in the fourth type of the book of Objectives (al-Maqasid) in his work titled Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul al-Shari'ah. Regarding applying the verse to this, there is a point for consideration, which you already know, so verify it.
