Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 58:

Page 29
﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm.﴾
This is a justification (ta'lil) for the two clauses ﴿I do not want any provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 57].

Here al-Razzaq (the Provider) carries a meaning that encompasses both wealth and feeding.

Al-Razzaq: the one who provides abundantly. Al-Quwwah (strength): al-qudrah (power).

Dhu al-quwwah: possessor of power. Among the characteristics of dhu is that it is attached to an important matter, so it is understood that the strength here is strength free from deficiencies.

Al-Matin: the firm, the mighty. Here it is a description of the possessor of strength, i.e., the one whose strength is firm. Al-Matin has been counted among His names, may He be exalted. Al-Ghazali said: "This returns to the meanings of power." In Ma'arij al-Nur, the explanation of the names reads: "Al-Matin: perfection in His strength such that it cannot be opposed and cannot be approached."

The meaning, then, is that He is absolutely self-sufficient, needing nothing, so His creating the creation is not to obtain any benefit for Himself, but for the cultivation of the cosmos and the operation of the order of civilization through following the law, which is comprised by the meaning of worship in His saying ﴿except that they worship Me﴾.

The mention of the name Allah in ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider﴾ is a departure from the expected form of speech, since what would be expected is: "Indeed, I am the Provider." He turned from the pronoun to the apparent name so that this sentence would be independent in its indication, because it was made to proceed in the manner of comprehensive speech and proverbs. The ya' of the first person was dropped from (ya'buduni) and (yut'imuni) for lightness, and its parallels in the Qur'an are numerous.

In His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ there is a mode of restriction (qasr) by the presence of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), i.e., there is no provider, nor possessor of strength, nor firm one, except Allah. It is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), i.e., apart from the idols that they worship.

The restriction is a restriction of singling out (qasr ifrad), by treating the polytheists in their associating their idols with Allah as one who claims that the idols are partners of Allah in His attributes, among which are provision, strength, and might,

Page 30
and this claim is refuted by this restriction. He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision; so seek provision from Allah and worship Him﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17], and He said: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should take from them anything, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj: 73].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 51, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, for those who did wrong there is a portion of punishment like the portion of their companions, so let them not ask Me to hasten it.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the sentence "And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me," in view of the fact that the purpose of its context is to nullify their worship of other than God. That is: if the polytheists do not single Me out for worship, then indeed for them is a portion of punishment like the portion of their companions. It alludes to what was mentioned earlier of the punishments by which the earlier nations were chastised, from His saying "They said: Indeed we have been sent to a people who are criminals" up to His saying "Indeed they were a people who were defiantly disobedient."

The meaning: when those who did wrong are matched with them, then indeed for them is a great share of punishment, like the share of those.

"Those who did wrong" are the polytheists among the Arabs, and wrongdoing (zulm) is associating partners with God.

The word dhanub, with a fatha on the dhal, is a large bucket with which the water-drawers draw water from the well, as occurs in the hadith of the dream: "Then Abu Bakr took it and drew one or two buckets (dhanub)." It is not called a dhanub unless it is full.

The statement is a parable (tamthil) for a state in which the share of those who did wrong among the Arabs is made equal to the shares of those who did wrong among the earlier nations, by the state of those who draw water from a single well, as they are equal in their portions of water. This is an expression of an intellectual image through a sensory one, and he applied to the earlier nations the description of the companions of those who did wrong, in view of the state that is compared to it, since it is the state of groups of water-drawers who accompany one another.

This parable admits of distribution, so that the polytheists may be likened to a group that came to the water, and the earlier nations may be likened to a group that preceded them to the water, and the portion of each group is likened to the bucket they take from the water.

ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbadah said, praising the king al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr and interceding with him on behalf of his brother Shas ibn ʿAbadah, who had fallen into his captivity together with the Banu Tamim on the day of ʿAyn Abagh:

"In every tribe you have dipped a bucket of favour, so Shas has earned a due bucket (dhunub) of your generosity."

When the king heard it, he said: "Yes, and more buckets (adhnibah)," and he released for him his brother Shas ibn ʿAbadah and those with him from the captives of Tamim.

This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). The purpose is that the polytheists should hear it, so it is an allusion (ta'rid), and in this sense the report was emphasized with inna, because they were denying the threat. For this reason the prohibition "so let them not ask Me to hasten it" follows upon the emphasis, because they used to ask for the punishment to be hastened mockingly and to indicate that it was a false promise. Thus in reality they were asking God Most High to hasten His threat.

The verb "hasten" (al-istiʿjal) is transitively extended to the pronoun of the Divine Name, whereas they were in fact asking it of the Prophet (ﷺ), to show that the Prophet (ﷺ) was informing about God Most High, as a rebuke to them and a warning of the threat. The yā' of the first person was omitted for lightness.

The prohibition (al-nahy) is used in the sense of mockery, to show the anger of God against them.

**[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 51, verse 60]**

﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from their day which they are promised.﴾

This is followed by another warning with "woe" (*al-waylu*), or it is an expression of rebuke.

*Al-waylu* means evil and bad condition. It was mentioned in His words ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. Its indefiniteness (*tankir*) is for magnification.

The statement may be understood as informing that a woe, meaning punishment and a bad condition, has occurred for them on the day they were threatened with it. It may also be understood as an expression of rebuke and of wonder at the bad state they are in on a day they were threatened with.

*Min* here is for the beginning of a figurative sense (*li-l-ibtida' al-majazi*), meaning: a bad condition resulting from their awaiting a punishment coming to them from the day they were threatened with.

[Page 32]

*Al-ladhina kafaru* (those who disbelieve): they are *al-ladhina zalamu* (those who wronged). He turned away from their pronoun to the apparent noun because it carries an emphasis on the preceding noun through a synonymous emphasis, along with what the attribute of disbelief implies of their failure to thank the Creator for His blessing.

The day they were promised is the time when the punishment descends. It may be meant as the Day of Resurrection, and it may be the descent of punishment in this world. Whichever it is, the content of this sentence differs from the content of the one before it.

The idafa (construction) of "day" to their pronoun is to indicate that it is specific to them, meaning that it is appointed for their recompense, just as "day" is idafa-ed to the pronoun of the believers in His words ﴿And the angels will meet them: "This is your day which you were promised."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103].

"Day" (*al-yawm*) applies to the Day of Resurrection, and it applies to the Day of Badr, in which God uprooted their power.

Since the pronoun in the idafa refers to specific disbelievers, namely the disbelievers of Makkah, it is preferred that the intended day is a day specific to them, and it is the Day of Badr, because the Day of Resurrection is not specific to them but is general to the disbelievers of all nations. This differs from the day in His words in Surat al-Anbiya', ﴿This is your day which you were promised﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103], because the pronoun of address in it refers to ﴿those for whom the best [reward] from Us has preceded﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], all of them.

Among the subtle points in the verse is the image of what will befall those who disbelieve because of their sins, and sins suit the well (*al-qalib*). Their dwelling on the Day of Badr was the well of Badr, into which the corpses of their leaders were thrown. This is the day in which Shaddad ibn Aws al-Laythi, known by the kunya Abu Bakr, said, mourning their dead:

"What is with the well, the well of Badr, of the bowls (*al-shizā*) adorned with humps?
It greets with safety Umm Bakr, and is there for me, after my people, any safety?"

It is possibly among what is included in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he stood over the well on the Day of Badr: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?"

[Page 33]

In His words ﴿from their day which they are promised﴾, together with His words at the beginning of the surah ﴿What you are promised is surely true﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 5], there is the return of the end to the beginning (*radd al-'ajz 'ala al-sadr*). In it is an announcement of the conclusion of the surah, and this is part of the excellence of the closing (*bara'at al-maqta'*).

[Page 34]

[Page 35]

**In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Tur.**

This surah was called, among the early scholars (*al-salaf*), "Surat al-Tur" without a waw before "al-Tur." In the chapter on circumambulation in al-Muwatta' there is a ḥadīth of Malik from Umm Salamah, who said: "I circumambulated while the Messenger of God was beside the House reciting by (*bi*) *al-Tur* ﴿and a written book﴾ [al-Tur: 2]," meaning he was reciting the surah of al-Tur. She did not mean he was reciting the verse, because the verse contains "wa-al-Tur" with a waw, and she did not mention the waw.

In the chapter on recitation in the Maghrib prayer in al-Muwatta' there is a ḥadīth of Malik: "From Jubayr ibn Mut'im, I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ recite by al-Tur in the Maghrib prayer."

In the commentary of Surat al-Tur in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, he said: "I heard the Prophet recite in the Maghrib prayer by al-Tur. When he reached this verse ﴿Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35] ﴿Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they are not certain﴾ [al-Tur: 36] ﴿Or with them are the treasuries of your Lord, or are they the controllers?﴾ [al-Tur: 37], my heart was about to fly." Jubayr ibn Mut'im was a polytheist who came to the Prophet ﷺ concerning the ransom of the captives of Badr, and he became Muslim that day.

Likewise, its naming was recorded in its translation in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, in the mushafs we have seen, and in many tafsir works. This is by naming through idafa, meaning "the surah that mentions al-Tur," just as one says "Surat al-Baqarah," "Surat al-Hudhud," and "Surat al-Mu'minun."

In the translation of this surah in the tafsir of Sahih al-Bukhari it is "Surat wa-al-Tur" with a waw, following the wording that occurs at its beginning, just as one says "Surat Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad."

It is a Makkan surah in its entirety by consensus.

It is the seventy-fifth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat Nuh and before Surat al-Mu'minun.

[Page 36]

The people of Madinah and Makkah counted its verses as forty-seven. The people of Syria and Kufa counted them as forty-nine, and the people of Basra counted them as forty-eight.

**The themes of this surah.** The first theme of this surah is the threat of the punishment of the Day of Resurrection for the polytheists who denied the Prophet ﷺ regarding what he brought, namely the affirmation of resurrection, and regarding the Qur'an that contains this. They said: "It is magic."

Its threat is set against the promise to the pious believers, the description of their bliss, the description of their remembrance with fear, and their praise of God for what He bestowed upon them. Then it moves to consoling the Prophet ﷺ, refuting their statements about him, and their waiting for his death.

It also includes their challenge, since they were unable to produce something like the Qur'an.

It refutes a mixture of their falsehoods: the return of creation, the sending of a Messenger who is not one of their great men, the claim that the angels are daughters of God, the plurality of gods, and it mentions their mockery of the threat.

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to leave them and not to grieve over that, for the threat will befall them in this world and then in the Hereafter. He was commanded to be patient, promised support, and commanded to thank his Lord at all times.
